name: Themba Dlamini
feedback:
D1: You catalogued five findings cleanly, and where you did report one you almost always quoted a real evidence line, which is exactly the habit we want: SQL injection (A03/CWE-89) off the concatenated WHERE clause, alg:none JWT acceptance (A07, you used CWE-345 where CWE-347 is the tighter fit but that is a defensible variant), no token expiry (A07/CWE-613 from exp:9999999999), XXE (A05/CWE-611), and the cookie with the secure flag false (A05/CWE-614). The problem is what is absent. You missed five of the ten substantiated findings: the unsalted MD5 hashing at line 66 (A02/CWE-916), the hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (CWE-798), the stored XSS posted to comments/post, the path traversal via files/?path=/etc/passwd (you folded that target into XXE, but the capture at 02:24:02 shows files/?path traversal as its own route, two routes one outcome), and the open redirect via ?next=. Each missing finding costs its share, so this row is roughly half. On the decoy you did the honest thing and ruled the base64url helper a false positive, good, but you analysed the wrong construct: the intended decoy is the HS256 verification branch that uses hash_equals(), and full credit needed you to name that branch and prove it safe at the mechanism level, that hash_equals is a constant-time comparison so it resists timing attacks, then pivot to the real bugs which are the alg:none branch and the hardcoded secret sitting right above it.

D2: This was the weakest deliverable. You showed real PoC artefacts, the admin'--+- payload, the alg:none token string, and the file:///etc/passwd entity, which is better than describing them, so the PoC row earned partial credit. But the chain is only four hops and you skipped recon (02:14:08), the failed guess (02:14:55), stored XSS (02:18:47), and open redirect (02:21:13), and you mis-reconciled the JWT hop to 02:16:04, which is actually the bulk-PII line returning 312 rows. The biggest loss is CVSS: there is not a single vector string anywhere in D2, and the key demands a complete vector per finding. For SQLi you should have written CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N around 9.1 with a one-sentence justification. A bare score earns half, no vector at all earns nothing, so you forfeited that whole row. Business impact in D2 was thin too: state 312 customers, PII plus financial, balances up to about 950k NGN summing to tens of millions, and tie it to BoltCash launching in roughly six weeks.

D3: Your remediation section is the standout and the reason this report is not lower. You ranked SQLi at 2 hours, XXE at 1 hour, JWT at 4 hours, and argued the order by effort-to-impact and breaking the chain first rather than by raw CVSS severity, which is precisely the risk-reduction-per-hour reasoning we ask for. Your two detection stopgaps are also strong: a WAF rule on alg:none with a 0.00% false-positive claim and a SIEM rule on the SYSTEM external-entity pattern at under 0.05%, both naming the exact pattern and a rate. Where you lost marks: the exec summary buries the headline, it ends on a compliance and rollout line when it should close on the customers-and-naira number a CFO can act on; your findings are not tied back to specific timestamps or file-and-line, so they read as a list rather than evidence-backed; and you never restated the disproved decoy in the report, which is a required line.

D4: Your strongest deliverable. You answered all four prompts with owned decisions, refusing the journalist, committing the unmodified audit trail to an immutable forensic locker regardless of management, keeping full evidentiary transparency on the colleague, and naming the one action you take no matter what. You cited ISC2 Canon I and Canon II by number and made them load-bearing, named NDPA 2023 by section tied to the 312 confirmed customers, and anchored to your own reconstruction including the ₦1,425,320.59 figure. To sharpen next time, lean on §40 (notify the NDPC within 72 hours) and §41 (notify affected data subjects on high risk) explicitly rather than §14, since those are the breach-duty sections.

No fabrication: your decoy call was honest and your figures trace to the exfil sample, so no penalty. The single most important thing to fix is evidence-and-CVSS density in D1 and D2: find all ten findings, quote the proving line for each, and defend a complete CVSS vector on every D2 finding. That alone would move you from the high-40s into the 60s.

name: Chinonyelum Cynthia Asogwa
feedback:
D1 is the standout. You catalogued all ten real findings and then some, and almost every row carries a quoted evidence line, the concatenated WHERE username = '" . $username . "' string for the SQLi, the alg:none acceptance for the JWT bypass, the file:///etc/passwd entity for the XXE, the 02:24:02 path traversal, the 02:21:13 open redirect, and the missing Secure/SameSite cookie. Your classes are mostly sound, and where you varied (MD5 as CWE-327 instead of 916, alg:none as CWE-345 instead of 347) those are defensible class variants, so you kept the marks. The decoy is handled exactly the way I wanted to see: you flagged the HS256 verification branch as suspicious, then proved it safe at the mechanism level by naming hash_equals as a constant-time comparison and correctly relocating the real bug to alg:none above it. That is honest work and it is what separates a real analyst from a checklist. The only soft spot in D1 is the method section, which reads thin against this specific pack.

D2 is where the report drops. Your chain only really ties two events to capture timestamps (SQLi at 02:15:31 and the 312-row export at 02:16:04), and the ordering is muddled, you place the XXE file read before the exfil and you leave the stored XSS (02:18:47), open redirect (02:21:13), and the /etc/passwd traversal (02:24:02) out of the chain entirely. The brief asked for hops three through eight each reconciled to a capture line, and you delivered roughly four. Your CVSS vectors are complete strings with the CVSS:3.1 prefix, which is good, but you only scored three findings and you gave the SQLi A:H when this is a read/bypass with no availability hit, so AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N would have been cleaner, and each vector needs a one-sentence justification you did not write. Business impact names 312 customers, balances in naira, and the BoltCash launch, but you never put a figure on it. Say tens of millions of naira with the sample max near 950,000 and state your assumptions, that earns more than a bare gesture at the number. You also missed the senior insight that a forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service, a scope change.

D3 is strong. The exec summary lands the 312-customers-and-naira headline, your six findings are tied to file and timestamp evidence and read cleanly for an engineer, you state the disproved decoy, and your earliest-break fix correctly points at the login query. Best of all, your remediation order is argued by risk reduction against estimated effort rather than CVSS alone, which is precisely the reasoning I was looking for. Two detection stopgaps with exact fields, patterns, and false-positive rates round it out well, though a JWT alg:none header rule would have been the third obvious one to name.

D4 is competent but incomplete. You answer all four prompts with owned decisions, your journalist stance and your evidence-preservation answer are mature, and you cite ISC2 Canon 1 by number and make it load-bearing. Two gaps cost you: you reference the NDPA 2023 in general but never name the section, you needed §40 (notify the NDPC within 72 hours) or §41 (notify affected data subjects on high risk) tied to the 312 customers, and you never anchor a sentence to your own specific Stage 2 work, you stay at "customer PII was exposed" instead of pointing at your SQLi bypass, the /etc/passwd read, or the 312-row export.

The single most important thing to fix is D2: rebuild the exploit chain so every hop from three to eight is in order and pinned to its exact capture timestamp, then attach a complete, justified CVSS vector to each finding rather than to three.

name: Samer Mohamed Badawy
missingPieces: Decoy analysis (hash_equals safe construct) absent across D1 and D3. Colleague prompt absent in D4. CVSS vector strings absent in D2 (bare scores only).
feedback:
Samer, you put together a broad catalogue and a readable report, but the marks come off because of evidence depth, the decoy, and one fabricated number, so let me walk you through it deliverable by deliverable.

D1: You found all ten vulnerabilities, which is genuinely good coverage, and your SQLi entry quoting the concatenation at 01-legacy-admin-login.php:39-43 is exactly the kind of proof I want. The problem is your OWASP mapping. You filed MD5 hashing, JWT alg:none, the hardcoded secret, and XXE all under A03 Injection, which is wrong. Unsalted MD5 is A02 Cryptographic Failures (CWE-916 or 759, not 327), alg:none is A07 Identification and Authentication Failures (CWE-347), the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 is A02 or A05 (CWE-798), and XXE is A05 (CWE-611). Lumping crypto and auth bugs into Injection reads like you guessed the category, and several findings carried a CWE with no quoted line, which costs you because the marks are for the proving line, not the label. The bigger miss is the decoy. The intended decoy was the hand-rolled crypto that is actually safe, specifically the HS256 verification branch using hash_equals(), which is a correct constant-time comparison, plus the base64url helpers which are just encoding. You were supposed to spot that tempting construct and prove it safe at the mechanism level. Instead you wrote "EXPLOITABLE, NOT A DECOY" about alg:none, which is just a real finding restated, so you never engaged the actual decoy at all and that whole row went to zero.

D2: Your chain is your strongest piece. The hops line up cleanly to the capture, 02:15:31 for the OR '1'='1 bypass, 02:16:04 for the 312 rows, 02:18:47 for the XSS beacon, 02:21:13 for the redirect, 02:24:02 for the /etc/passwd read, and you showed real payloads rather than describing them. Two things hurt you. You gave bare CVSS scores (9.8, 9.0, 8.7, 7.7) with no vector strings, and a number without a vector is half credit at best. For the SQLi you want something like AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N around 9.1 with one sentence of justification, and the senior insight is that the forged super_admin token reaching the shared /api/v1/internal service flips scope to S:C. The other thing is your business impact figure. You stated ₦47,811,520.39 down to the kobo for 312 customers. That number cannot exist. The exfil sample is twenty placeholder rows standing in for the real export, with balances up to roughly 950,000 NGN, so the honest answer is to state your assumption out loud, for example 312 customers times a sample-derived average gives tens of millions of naira, and tie it to BoltCash launching in about six weeks. Inventing a kobo-precise total that does not trace to the sample is a fabrication, and it cost you a flat penalty.

D3: This was your best deliverable. The exec summary lands the 312 records and naira headline a CFO can act on, the Griot threat model with the Tor exit node is concrete, and importantly you argued remediation by effort to risk, the four-hour parameterised query as highest ROI ahead of the eight-hour JWT fix, which is exactly the reasoning I wanted rather than ranking by raw CVSS. Your two detection stopgaps name real fields and patterns with false-positive rates, which most people skip. Watch the "0% false positive" claim on the alg:none rule, nothing is truly zero, give an honest low estimate instead. And the decoy problem follows you here too, the report should state the disproved safe construct, not declare a live bug "not a decoy."

D4: Good own voice and you cited ISC2 Canon IV by number and made it carry weight. Two real gaps. You never answered the colleague prompt, the senior who is about to take the fall and how you handle evidence that could protect or implicate them, which is a quarter of the exercise. And your NDPA citation is wrong. You wrote Section 34, but the breach duties are §40 (notify the NDPC within 72 hours) and §41 (notify affected data subjects on high risk), with §44 as the fine ceiling. Get the section right because that is the load-bearing part. Also your breach date drifted to 2024, the capture window is 02:14 to 02:31 UTC.

The single most important thing to fix: engage the decoy honestly. Open the hash_equals verification branch, state that constant-time comparison is correct and the branch is safe, and point the danger at alg:none and the hardcoded secret instead. Proving a safe thing safe is worth more than relabelling a known bug, and it is the difference between a thorough analyst and a checklist one.

name: Precious Kelechi Okafor
feedback:
Strong capstone overall, and the strongest part is your D1 catalogue. You found all ten substantiated bugs plus a bonus username enumeration finding, and almost every row carries the correct class and CWE next to a real quoted evidence line: SQLi as A03/CWE-89 with the WHERE username concatenation at login.php:64-67, MD5 at line 66, alg:none at lines 48-50 with the actual "if alg === none return payload" branch quoted, the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 at lines 30/38, stored XSS pinned to the 02:18:47 capture with the cookie beacon payload, and XXE with the file:///etc/passwd entity. That is evidence-led work, not label guessing, which is exactly what earns marks here. Your decoy handling is excellent: you correctly picked the hash_equals verification branch, proved it SAFE at the mechanism level by explaining constant-time comparison defeats timing analysis, and you also disproved the persistent RCE claim by noting the file access was read-only with no write handlers. One small thing to tighten: you tagged missing token expiry as A04 Insecure Design where the key expects A07, a defensible variant but be deliberate about it.

D2 is where you lost the most ground. Your CVSS work is genuinely good, complete vector strings on eight findings each with a justifying sentence, and your SQLi auth-bypass vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N lines up with the expected ~9.1, so keep doing that. The weakness is the chain itself. You collapsed seven hops into four and mis-reconciled two of them. 02:16:04 in the capture is the 312-row bulk PII pull, not a JWT forgery, and your XXE timestamp of 02:22:15 does not exist in the capture, the file read is at 02:24:02. Your path traversal PoC also shows ?path=customer_pii_export.db when the proving capture line is ?path=/etc/passwd with the body beginning root:x:0:0. Next time, reconcile every hop to the exact timestamp in 02-attacker-http-capture.txt and keep the recon, failed guess, bulk PII, XSS and open redirect hops as distinct steps rather than folding them together. Your business impact was handled well: 312 customers, 67.79M NGN derived from the sample average with the assumption stated openly, which is the right instinct.

D3 is polished and mostly hits. The threat model, the disproved decoy, the two detection stopgaps with exact patterns and false-positive rates (alg:none base64 header at 0 percent, the traversal/XXE SIEM query at under 1 percent), and especially the remediation order argued by Risk Reduced Per Hour are all strong. Two gaps cost you. Your exec summary reads technical and compliance-heavy rather than something a CFO can act on, and it ends on a bare naira figure instead of the customers-and-naira headline. More importantly, you never name parameterising the login query as the earliest break that kills the chain at hop 3, you actually rank the SQL fix third behind JWT and XXE. The whole point of the earliest-break analysis is that fixing hop 3 collapses everything downstream, so call that out explicitly.

D4 is complete and well done: all four prompts answered with owned decisions, Canon II cited by number and made load-bearing against the cover-up pressure, NDPA 2023 Section 40 tied to the 312 records, and your own voice anchored to your real findings at 02:15:31 and 02:16:04. Watch the length, you ran near 580 words against a 300 to 500 ceiling. The single most important thing to fix is your exploit chain in D2: reconcile every hop to its true capture timestamp and stop collapsing distinct steps, because a mis-timed or invented hop undercuts an otherwise excellent report.

name: Temitope Mustapha
feedback: D1 is strong and is where most of your marks came from. You catalogued nine findings and almost all carried a real quoted evidence line with file and line numbers, which is exactly what this row rewards. SQLi (CWE-89, the concatenated WHERE username query), unsalted MD5, JWT alg:none, the hardcoded sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 secret, missing token expiry, XXE, the insecure cookie and open redirect are all there with proof. Two real problems cost you. First, path traversal (files/?path=/etc/passwd returning root:x:0:0: at 02:24:02) is missing entirely as its own finding, and it is a distinct route from the XXE even though both land on /etc/passwd. Second, you logged Reflected XSS pointing at the login error echo, but the actual finding in this pack is STORED XSS posted to comments/post at 02:18:47 with a cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443, so you labeled the wrong class and cited the wrong line for a vuln that genuinely exists elsewhere. A few of your OWASP buckets are also swapped (alg:none and no-expiry are A07 not A01, the hardcoded secret is closer to A02/A05 than A07), though your CWE ids carried those rows. Your decoy handling was excellent and earned full credit: you found hash_equals, called it not exploitable, and proved it at the mechanism level as constant-time rather than inventing an exploit, which is exactly the honest call. D2 is your weakest deliverable. Your chain is only five hops and skips the stored XSS step entirely, and it folds the path traversal file read into the XXE hop so two separate routes read as one. Reconcile every hop to its own capture line and keep traversal and XXE as parallel routes to the same outcome. Your CVSS work is good where it exists, three complete vector strings with justifications, but you only scored three findings, so most of your catalogue has no vector at all, and that is what held this row down. Score a complete AV:.../A:... vector for each substantive finding, not just three. Small note: your F-01 vector used A:H for ~9.8 where SQLi here is closer to A:N at ~9.1 since you are reading and writing data, not affecting availability. Business impact was solid: 312 customers, PII plus financial, a ₦35M figure with a stated breakdown, and the BoltCash six-week tie, and your numbers trace to the exfil sample, so no fabrication there. D3 is polished. The threat model, evidence-linked findings, remediation code and the disproved decoy are all present, and crucially your remediation table is argued by risk-reduction-per-hour with explicit effort hours, not by raw severity, with the parameterised login query as the earliest-break fix that kills the chain at hop three. That is the prioritisation reasoning this row wants and you nailed it. Both detection stopgaps name exact fields and patterns with false-positive rates, which most reports forget. D4 is your best work and full marks: all four prompts answered with owned decisions, ISC2 Canons I and II cited by number and actually load-bearing, NDPA 2023 Section 40 tied directly to the 312 customers and the 72-hour duty, and a genuine anchor back to your own SQLi/MD5 root-cause analysis in your own voice. The single most important thing to fix next time is D2 completeness: surface every hop including stored XSS, split traversal from XXE, and attach a full CVSS vector to every substantive finding rather than three.
missingPieces: D1 missing path traversal as a finding; stored XSS mislabeled as reflected with wrong evidence line. D2 missing stored XSS hop, conflates path traversal into XXE, CVSS vectors on only 3 of the findings.

name: Folorunso Victoria Morenikeji
feedback:
D1: This is a clean, evidence-led catalogue for the findings you did report. Every one of your six findings quotes the exact proving artefact, the SQL concatenation line, the alg:none branch at line 30 plus Token 2, the ENTITY SYSTEM line, the cookie-stealing script body, the next= redirect lines, and the MD5() call, which is exactly the discipline we want. The problem is coverage: you stopped at six. You missed the hardcoded/guessable JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (CWE-798), the no-token-expiry flaw (CWE-613, the giveaway is exp:9999999999 plus Token 1 having no exp at all), the session cookie set with no Secure/SameSite (CWE-614/1275), and, importantly, path traversal as its own finding (CWE-22). You folded /etc/passwd entirely into XXE, but the capture at 02:24:02 shows files/?path=/etc/passwd, a separate route to the same file read, and that is finding number eight, not part of the XXE. Two routes, one outcome, both get listed. Your class labels are mostly fine: alg:none as A02 and MD5 as CWE-327 are defensible variants even though the key prefers A07/CWE-916. Your decoy work is the best part of the whole submission. You picked the right construct, the hash_equals HS256 branch, proved it safe at the mechanism level with the constant-time argument, and correctly called it a false positive rather than inventing an exploit. Full marks there.

D2: Your PoCs are genuinely strong, real HTTP bodies, the verbatim alg:none token string, the full XXE XML, and actual CSV rows, artefacts shown not described. But you collapsed the intrusion into four hops and that cost you. The real chain has the recon at 02:14:08, the failed guess at 02:14:55, the stored XSS at 02:18:47, and the open redirect at 02:21:13, none of which appear in your chain even though XSS and open redirect are in your own D1. A reconstruction that skips two confirmed attacker actions is not the full picture. Your CVSS vectors are complete and justified, which is what earns the marks, but watch the SQLi vector: you set A:H when an auth-bypass login query does not take down availability, so A:N is the defensible call there. Business impact is handled well, 312 customers, the stated 201,800 NGN average extrapolated to roughly 63M, and the BoltCash six-week tie-in, and crucially you showed your assumption rather than asserting a bare number.

D3: Your strongest deliverable. The exec summary is genuinely CFO-readable and ends on the 312-customers-and-63M headline, the threat model correctly flags the Tor exit node and the shared auth trust with the internal API, and your remediation table is exactly right: you ranked the sub-one-hour JWT deletion and the two-hour XXE config change above the one-day SQL parameterisation, argued by effort and risk-reduction-per-hour rather than raw CVSS, which is the whole point of that row. Both detection stopgaps name a concrete field and pattern (decoded alg:none header, the OR '1'='1 tautology regex on the login POST) with an FP rate. One nudge: parameterising the login query is the true earliest-break that kills the chain at hop three, so consider whether it deserves to sit even higher than third on pure chain-breaking grounds. Findings list here only carries four of your six, so engineering loses sight of the redirect and MD5 issues.

D4: All four prompts answered with owned decisions, you ignore the journalist and route to PR, you commit only verifiable facts to writing under discovery, you refuse to bury the lifecycle timeline that implicates the colleague, and you make regulatory disclosure your non-negotiable. Canon II is quoted and load-bearing, and you anchored it to your own exfil-sample mapping, which is exactly the personal voice we ask for. The one gap that cost you: you named the NDPA 2023 72-hour NDPC duty but never cited it by section. Write §40 (notify the NDPC within 72 hours) and, since this is high financial risk, §41 (notify the affected data subjects) next time, tied to the 312. That section number is what turns a good answer into a defensible one.

The single most important thing to fix: report the whole attack surface. You proved you can quote evidence cleanly, so the gap is completeness, catalogue all ten findings (you left four on the table) and reconcile every capture line in the chain (you dropped the XSS and open-redirect hops). A thorough catalogue is what separates this from a top mark.
missingPieces: D1 missing four findings: hardcoded JWT secret (CWE-798), no token expiry (CWE-613), cookie no Secure/SameSite (CWE-614/1275), and path traversal as a standalone finding (CWE-22, capture 02:24:02). D2 chain omits recon 02:14:08, failed guess 02:14:55, stored XSS hop 02:18:47, open redirect hop 02:21:13. D4 names NDPA 72h duty but no section number (§40/§41).

name: Ugwu Godsfavour Somtochukwu
feedback: D1: You catalogued eight of the ten findings, and the strong ones are well done. SQLi at lines 54-57 with the 02:15:31 capture, the alg:none branch at lines 37-39 tied to Token 2, MD5 at line 56, XXE, stored XSS, path traversal, open redirect and the cookie flags all carry a real evidence line plus an OWASP and CWE id, which is exactly what I want to see. A few class ids drift from the key (CWE-328 for the weak hash, CWE-345 for the JWT) but those are defensible variants so I did not punish them. Two real findings are missing as their own rows: the hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (CWE-798) and the no-expiry tokens (CWE-613), and that is where the bigger problem is. Your decoy section is wrong. The intended decoy was the SAFE hand-rolled crypto, specifically the HS256 verification branch that uses hash_equals(), which is a correct constant-time comparison, and the b64url helpers, which are just encoding. The honest answer was to point at hash_equals, prove it is fine at the mechanism level, and say the real bugs are alg:none and the hardcoded secret sitting above it. Instead you took the hardcoded secret, which is a genuine vulnerability, and labelled it a decoy that did not matter. You dismissed a real finding rather than disproving a safe one, so that row scores zero and you also lose finding 4. Next time, separate "looks dangerous but is provably safe" (hash_equals) from "is dangerous" (the secret); they are not the same thing. D2: The chain is the strongest part of the pack. Real request bodies, the actual base64 Token 2 string decoded, the XSS payload and the traversal path are all shown rather than described, and most hops reconcile to the right capture timestamp. The S:C scope change on the alg:none hop is the senior insight and you got it. Two things cost you. First, you invented a capture line: the XXE hop cites 04-import-xxe.xml at 2024-06-04T02:23:41Z, but that file has no timestamp anywhere in the evidence pack and the capture window is 02:14 to 02:31 UTC, so that is a fabricated evidence line and it triggers a flat five point penalty. Do not manufacture precision; if a route has no capture line, say so and reconcile it as a parallel route to the 02:24:02 /etc/passwd read, which is what it is. Second, the business impact has no money in it. You reference 05-exfil-sample.csv and say "over 300 records" but give no naira figure, no tens-of-millions exposure, no ~950k NGN max balance, and no tie to BoltCash launching in six weeks. State your assumptions and put a number on it. Your CVSS vectors are all complete strings, which earns most of that row, but the justifications are one phrase each and a couple of metrics are loose (SQLi as A:H where availability is not really hit). D3: Good engineering register, a clear threat model map, the vulnerable login line quoted verbatim and the PDO fix shown. The exec summary does not land the headline though; it ends on lateral movement and data loss instead of the customers-and-naira line a CFO can act on, so tighten that to "312 customers, PII and financial data, tens of millions of naira at stake." The remediation plan is ordered sensibly but it is argued by impact, not by risk-reduction-per-hour, and that is the specific thing this row marks. Say plainly that parameterising the login query is a few hours of work and breaks the chain at hop 3, so it ranks above a higher-CVSS fix that takes weeks. That framing is missing and it caps the remediation row. Your detection stopgaps name good exact patterns (OR '1'='1, <!ENTITY, SYSTEM "file://") but none carry an expected false-positive rate, which is half the point of a stopgap, so add one per rule. The disproved decoy is not restated here either. D4: This is the weakest deliverable and it reads like a generic disclosure essay rather than an answer to the scenario. You did not engage the four prompts: nothing on what you tell the journalist you know and why, nothing on what you will and will not put in writing, nothing on handling evidence that could protect or implicate the colleague about to take the fall, and no single action you take regardless of your manager. One full paragraph is also duplicated word for word. You cite ISC2 Canon 1 and 2 by number and make them load-bearing, which is good, but the NDPA reference has no section: name §40 (notify the NDPC within 72 hours) and §41 (notify the 312 affected data subjects on high risk). Anchor at least one sentence to your own Stage 2 work, for example the 312-row export and the alg:none forgery you documented. The single most important thing to fix: stop dismissing real bugs as decoys and stop inventing evidence lines. The decoy was the safe hash_equals branch, the hardcoded secret is a finding, and the XXE has no 02:23:41 timestamp; getting those three straight would have moved you up a band on its own.

name: fatokunbo samuel
feedback:
This is one of the strongest Stage 2 capstones I have marked, and the score reflects that, but there are a couple of precise errors I want you to fix so it is airtight next time.

D1: Excellent catalogue. You captured all ten substantiated findings, each with the OWASP 2021 category, a CWE id, and a quoted proving line: SQLi (A03/CWE-89) with the concatenated WHERE clause and the 02:15:31 admin' OR '1'='1, unsalted MD5 (A02/CWE-916), alg:none accepted (CWE-347) quoting the actual jwt_verify branch, the hardcoded sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 secret (CWE-798) with the dead "rotate before prod" comment, no token expiry (CWE-613), stored XSS (CWE-79) with the cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443, XXE (CWE-611), path traversal (CWE-22) ending root:x:0:0:, open redirect (CWE-601), and the cookie missing Secure/SameSite (CWE-614). The decoy work is exactly what we wanted: you named the hash_equals HS256 branch, proved it safe at the mechanism level (constant-time comparison), and pointed at the real bug two lines above it. The only thing keeping D1 off full marks is that you fold MD5 and the secret both under A02 without noting the defensible A05 variant, and there is no method section inside D1 itself describing how you worked this specific pack. Add a short three-line method paragraph next time.

D2: The chain is clean and reconciled hop by hop to capture lines (02:15:31 SQLi, 02:16:04 the 312 rows, 02:18:47 XSS, 02:21:13 redirect, then the file reads), and your PoCs are shown verbatim rather than described. feedback: Strong, broad catalogue let down by the one judgement call that this stage was built around. On D1 you found essentially all ten substantiated findings and tied most to a real evidence anchor: SQLi at 01-legacy-admin-login.php line 58 (A03/CWE-89), MD5 at line 59, alg:none at lines 42-46, the hardcoded secret at line 23, open redirect at line 80, stored XSS at the 02:18:47 capture, XXE at the import artefact, path traversal at 02:24:02, and the cookie flags at line 76. That is good coverage and earns the bulk of D1. Two things cost you: the no-expiry finding is classed CWE-339 (predictable RNG), which is the wrong class, the correct one is CWE-613, and your A04 tags on the cookie and expiry findings should be A05 and A07. The bigger miss is the decoy. The construct you were meant to adjudicate is the SAFE hand-rolled crypto, specifically the HS256 verification branch that uses hash_equals() for a constant-time comparison, plus the base64url encode/decode helpers, none of which is a weakness. You never mention hash_equals or constant-time comparison anywhere. Instead you took alg:none, which is a genuine bug, and labelled it the decoy while calling it exploitable. The honest answer was to quote the hash_equals branch and prove at the mechanism level that it is fine, then point out that the real bugs (alg:none and the hardcoded secret) sit right above it. That row scored zero. On D2 your chain is well sequenced and reconciled to the real capture timestamps, and your CVSS strings are complete vectors with justifications, which is exactly what we want; note the SQLi should read A:N not A:H since reading and bypassing auth does not break availability. The problem is the SSRF finding and its 9.9 vector: you cite a server response "Verified, the flag has been placed in the answer box" and claim IAM credential theft and full cloud account compromise, but the import.xml in the pack points at file:///etc/passwd, the same target as the path traversal, not the AWS metadata service. There is no capture line proving any SSRF to 169.254.169.254. That invented exploit and the invented cloud blast radius is a fabrication, and it also dragged your business impact off course: you landed on roughly 1.56M naira when the exfil sample shows balances up to about 950k each across 312 customers, which is tens of millions, and the real impact story is the 312 PII rows weeks before the BoltCash launch, not cloud takeover. For that fabrication I applied the flat five point penalty. On D3 the threat model is clean and your remediation table genuinely argues by risk reduction per hour with effort estimates, which is the senior move most people skip, so credit there. But your exec summary admits it is technical rather than something a CFO can act on and it does not end on the customers-and-naira headline, your "why this is not a decoy" section defends alg:none instead of disproving the safe construct, and you named alg:none as the first fix when the earliest break is parameterising the login query, which kills the chain at hop 3 before any token forgery matters. Your two detection stopgaps do carry exact regex and false-positive rates, which is good, though I would rather have seen the inbound alg:none header alert and the OR '1'='1 login-body rule than a stopgap for the SSRF you could not prove. D4 is your best work: all four prompts answered with owned decisions, Canon III cited by number and made load-bearing, and a clean anchor to your own 05-exfil-sample.csv and the 312 records. The one gap is the NDPA citation, you reference "Sections 30-35" loosely rather than the actual breach duties, which are §40 (notify the NDPC within 72 hours) and §41 (notify affected data subjects on high risk). Cite those by number next time. The single most important thing to fix: when a brief hints that one construct looks unsafe but is fine, slow down and prove the safe thing safe at the mechanism level, and never manufacture an exploit or an impact figure that the evidence pack does not support.

feedback:
Strong, well-organised capstone, but the marks are pulled down by one fabrication and a couple of missed items, so read this carefully.

D1: You catalogued nine findings, each with an OWASP category, a CWE, and an evidence pointer, which is the right shape. The class slips are mostly defensible (CWE-328 for the MD5 hashing where I would have taken CWE-916/759, and A01/CWE-345 for alg:none where A07/CWE-347 is cleaner), so I did not punish those hard. The real gap is that you missed an entire substantial finding: the hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 sitting around lines 30 and 38 (CWE-798), which is one of the seven core bugs, not an optional extra. The single best thing you did anywhere in this submission is the decoy: you correctly identified the hand-rolled crypto, pinned hash_equals as constant-time, and disproved the timing-attack false positive at the mechanism level while noting the real bugs (alg:none and the secret) live in the same file. That is exactly the judgement we are testing, full credit there. Your method section was generic ("code review plus automated scanning"); next time describe what you actually did against this pack, for example which capture timestamps you replayed and which token you decoded.

D2: This is where it costs you. Your real hops (SQLi 02:15:31, the 312-row pull at 02:16:04, traversal at 02:24:02) are reconciled correctly, but you invented two capture timestamps that do not exist in 02-attacker-http-capture.txt: 02:27:15 for the XXE hop and 02:30:51 for the exfil. The capture runs 02:14 to 02:31 and the file read at 02:24:02 is the terminal event, the XXE is a parallel route to the same /etc/passwd, not a later line. Inventing capture lines is a fabrication, so that row drops and I applied the flat five-point penalty. The honest move was to write "XXE via import.php is a parallel route to the same outcome as the 02:24:02 traversal, no separate capture line" and leave it there. You also dropped the stored XSS (02:18:47) and open redirect (02:21:13) out of the chain entirely, and you never connected the forged super_admin token to the shared /api/v1/internal service, which is the scope-change (S:C) senior insight. On the plus side your CVSS work is genuinely good: complete vectors with justifications on every finding, which most submissions do not manage, though your SQLi vector uses A:H where A:N is correct. Business impact was excellent, 312 customers, naira figures, a stated extrapolation assumption, and the BoltCash six-week tie.

D3: Your best deliverable. The exec summary lands jargon-free and closes on the ₦63m across 312 rows headline a CFO can act on, the "Griot" threat model is a nice touch, findings are engineering-readable, and the disproved decoy is restated. Most importantly you argued remediation by effort-to-risk ("allocate engineering hours where they prevent the most damage, rather than blindly fixing by severity scores alone") rather than raw CVSS, which is exactly what we look for, and both detection stopgaps name an exact pattern (the alg:none header regex, the OR tautology) with a false-positive rate. I docked only lightly because the exploit chain you carried in still misses the XSS and redirect hops.

D4: All four prompts answered with owned decisions, and Canon 3 is cited by number and load-bearing against the colleague conflict, good. Two clear misses: you named the NDPA 2023 and the duty to notify but gave no section, so cite §40 (notify the NDPC within 72 hours) and §41 (notify the 312 affected data subjects on high risk), and tie it to that exact customer count. And nothing anchored back to your own Stage 2 findings; one sentence like "the export I traced at 02:16:04 is the PII that triggers §40" would have closed that.

Single most important fix: never invent an evidence line. If a hop has no capture timestamp, say so plainly. That one habit cost you more than any missing finding here.

name: Oluwafemi Akinkoye
feedback: Akinkoye, this is a strong, careful submission, and your D3 in particular is some of the best prioritisation work in this batch. D1: your catalogue is thorough and evidence-led. You quoted the exact proving line for the SQL injection (A03, CWE-89), the unsalted MD5 hashing, the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (CWE-798), the missing token expiry (CWE-613), the open redirect (CWE-601), the insecure cookie flags (CWE-614), and the XXE entity (A05, CWE-611), which is exactly the class plus evidence pairing we want, and the MD5 CWE-328 is a defensible variant of the tighter CWE-916. Two real gaps. The XSS you listed is the reflected error-message reflection, but the substantiated one is the STORED XSS posted to comments/post at 02:18:47 that beacons the admin cookie to 185.220.101.9:8443, so add that. More important, you inverted the decoy: the alg:none branch you called the decoy is a real critical finding, because the source comment shows those tokens are honoured by the shared /api/v1/internal service and 03-tokens Token 2 is a live alg:none token, so it is exploitable across the system, not safe. The actual decoy is the HS256 verify branch that uses hash_equals(), a correct constant-time comparison, which is the genuinely safe construct you were meant to clear. Your instinct to ask whether a construct is really reachable was the right skill, you just aimed it at the wrong target. D2: the chain is mostly in order and each hop you included reconciles to a real capture timestamp, and your PoCs are verbatim requests rather than descriptions. You are missing two hops, the stored XSS at 02:18:47 and the open redirect at 02:21:13. Your CVSS vectors are complete strings with justifications, but check the SQL injection vector: you wrote A:H for 9.8 when the bypass reads and writes data without affecting availability, so A:N and roughly 9.1 is the defensible value. Your business impact is excellent, you carried the 312 records, averaged the exfil sample to about 64.3 million naira with your assumptions shown, and tied it to the six-week BoltCash window. One framing note, recasting the broken-auth finding as a PHPSESSID session weakness under-sells the real critical, which is the forged-token path through the shared internal API. D3: this is your standout. The executive summary is jargon-free and lands on the customers-and-naira headline, the threat model is tight, and your remediation order is exactly what the brief rewards: you ranked the few-hours SQL injection fix first because it breaks the chain at the entry point and argued it by risk reduction per hour rather than raw CVSS, and both detection stopgaps name a concrete pattern and a false-positive estimate. The one carry-over is that the decoy you state as disproved is the wrong one, correct it to the hash_equals branch. D4: strong and in your own voice. You answered all four prompts with owned decisions, cited Canon I and Canon III by number and made them load-bearing, and anchored to the exfil sample. To get the last marks, name the NDPA breach duty by section: section 40 requires notifying the NDPC within 72 hours and section 41 requires notifying the affected data subjects given the high-risk PII. The single most important thing to fix is the decoy: alg:none is a real cross-service vulnerability, and the safe construct you were meant to clear is the constant-time hash_equals comparison. Get that right and this report sits at the top of the cohort.

D1 catalogues seven of the ten real findings (SQL injection A03/CWE-89, unsalted MD5 A02, alg:none A07/CWE-347, no token expiry CWE-613, the hardcoded secret which you correctly quote as sankofa-legacy-admin-2019, insecure cookie flags CWE-614, and open redirect CWE-601), and you nailed the decoy by naming hash_equals and proving it constant-time and safe at the mechanism level, which is exactly right and earns full decoy credit. What holds D1 back is that you never quote a single code line or capture timestamp for any finding, so most rows fall to half credit because proof beats the label, and you completely miss three real bugs: the stored XSS in comments (capture 02:18:47, cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443), the XXE in 04-import-xxe.xml reading file:///etc/passwd, and the path traversal at files/?path=/etc/passwd returning root:x:0:0. Findings 7 through 12 are mostly padding and token-lifecycle restatements rather than new bugs, so they did not lift the score. D2 is your strongest work: the hops reconcile cleanly to the real capture lines (recon 02:14:08, SQLi 02:15:31, bulk PII 02:16:04 at 312 rows, stored XSS 02:18:47, open redirect 02:21:13, file read 02:24:02), you give verbatim payloads for the SQLi and the XSS beacon, and your impact ties 312 customers to roughly 28 million naira with a stated averaging assumption, which is the right instinct. Fix the SQLi CVSS: it should be AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N for about 9.1, not A:H, because the bypass does not touch availability. D3 is where the report goes wrong, because it describes a different scenario built around XXE plus an IMDSv2/SSRF cloud-credential leak and a JWT pipeline, and the canonical Sankofa findings (SQLi login, the XSS beacon, the /etc/passwd path traversal, the 312-row export) are largely absent; the exec summary never lands on a customers-and-naira headline. More seriously, your decoy section invents a disproof: there is no admin login at 10.0.4.16, no MFA-log correlation, and no SSRF-to-IMDS evidence anywhere in this pack, and the real safe construct you should have disproved is the hash_equals branch you already correctly identified in D1. Inventing the IMDS/SSRF finding and the MFA-log decoy correlation is fabrication, so that row scores zero and a flat five-point penalty applies; the honest move is to say plainly that no such evidence exists in the pack. Your remediation is genuinely ordered by effort and risk reduction per hour, and your two detection stopgaps name a log field and a false-positive rate, both of which are credited. D4 is excellent and almost saves the day: own voice throughout, all four prompts answered, ISC2 canons cited by number (1 and 2) and load-bearing, NDPA Section 40 breach notification tied directly to the 312 customers and to the exfil you proved in D2, and the one action you own (forcing DPO and legal to proceed with mandatory notification regardless of your manager) is exactly the spine the prompt wanted. I looked hard for a way to round the overall higher and the D2 and D4 strength is real, but the missing third of D1, the unquoted evidence, and the fabricated D3 decoy genuinely cap it where it sits. The single most important fix: stop writing about a different XML/IMDS scenario in D3 and ground every finding in the actual Sankofa capture lines and source you already cited in D2, and never invent a disproof when the safe construct is the hash_equals comparator.

Your CVSS vectors are complete and the SQLi vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at 9.1 matches the key exactly, but you give no justifying sentence per vector, so the vector row scores at half rather than full. The threat model table, the evidence-tied findings, the correctly disproved decoy, the earliest-break framing at the authentication layer, and above all the remediation order built on risk reduction per hour of effort rather than CVSS severity, with MD5 deliberately placed last because of migration cost, all hit the mark, and your two detection stopgaps both give an exact field and a false-positive rate. D1 findings: you documented one vulnerability properly, the SQL injection in the login query, and you did it well. You mapped it to A03 and CWE-89, you quoted the vulnerable concatenated query, and you tied it to real evidence with the mysql-general.log timestamps, the backup.sql schema, and the exfil-sample.csv. You did show one good instinct, the lateral move where the recovered token is reused against /api/v1/internal to pull 312 customer rows, which is the senior scope-change insight, and your impact write-up is genuinely strong: 312 customers, balances from 6,400 up to 950,000 NGN, the tens-of-millions exposure, and the BoltCash launch in six weeks all stated with assumptions. That impact reasoning is the best part of the submission. On D1 you catalogued every one of the ten core findings with the correct class, a defensible CWE, and a quoted evidence line: SQL injection F-01 CWE-89 at login.php:64-67 reconciled to capture [02:15:31], unsalted MD5 F-02 CWE-916 at line 66, alg:none F-03 CWE-347 at lines 48-49 with Token 2, the hardcoded secret F-04 (CWE-321 is a fine variant of 798), no expiry F-05 CWE-613, the Secure-flag gap F-06 CWE-614, open redirect F-07 CWE-601 at [02:21:13], stored XSS F-09 CWE-79 at [02:18:47], path traversal F-10 CWE-22 at [02:24:02] with the root:x:0:0 body, and XXE F-11 CWE-611 from the import file, plus a legitimate bonus reflected XSS. Your decoy handling is sound work: you took the tempting XSS-steals-the-JWT claim and disproved it at the mechanism level with RFC 6265 and the HttpOnly seventh parameter, which is exactly the kind of proof the exercise rewards, and you correctly treated alg:none as a real vulnerability rather than the decoy. The one thing that keeps D1 off a perfect mark is that the canonical safe construct here is the constant-time hash_equals branch of the HS256 verify path, so naming and proving that specific construct safe would have been the textbook answer. D2 is excellent on PoC quality, with verbatim payloads, a working alg:none forge script, and the exact XXE document, and your CVSS vectors carry justifying sentences. Two things cost you here: your SQLi vector uses A:H for a 9.8 when the auth bypass does not touch availability, so the correct vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1, and your main chain narrative drops the stored-XSS and open-redirect steps down into the findings table rather than threading them as hops. Your impact is well quantified with 312 records and the NGN 6,400 to 950,000 range, but it stops short of summing the high-balance accounts into the tens-of-millions exposure and does not tie the window to the BoltCash launch, which is where the business punch lands. D3 reads like a real report: a jargon-free executive summary that ends on customers and naira, a genuine threat model with trust boundaries, evidence-tied findings, a correct decoy restatement, and a clean earliest-break fix at the SQL parameterisation. The row that holds D3 back is remediation order: you state up front that you prioritised by severity, exploitation ease, and active use, which is essentially CVSS-led, where the exercise wants ordering by effort-to-risk (cheap high-impact fixes first), so that row is capped. Your two detection stopgaps are specific and well chosen, naming the username and password fields and the alg header, but neither carries an actual false-positive-rate estimate, which is the detail the rubric asks for. D4 is the cleanest part of the submission: you answer all four prompts in your own voice, you make Canon 1 load-bearing with Canon 2 in support, and you correctly cite NDPA 2023 Section 40 for the 72-hour NDPC notification plus the high-risk data-subject duty, all anchored to the 312 affected customers. Nothing here is fabricated; every evidence line and figure traces to the pack, so there is no penalty. The single most important fix is to reorder your remediation by effort-to-risk rather than CVSS severity, leading with the one-line prepared-statement fix and the secret rotation as cheap high-impact wins, and pair each detection stopgap with a concrete false-positive-rate estimate.

name: CH PAVANI PRIYA
feedback: D1 is a strong catalogue on the core seven. name: Hope David Michael

SQL injection (A03/CWE-89, lines 62-67, capture 02:15:31), JWT alg:none (A07/CWE-347, Token 2), XXE (A05/CWE-611), path traversal (A01/CWE-22, /files/?path=/etc/passwd at 02:24:02) and open redirect (A01/CWE-601, 02:21:13) are all correct and well sourced, and CWE-327 for the unsalted MD5 is a defensible variant of CWE-916. What cost you was three missing findings: the hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (CWE-798, ~line 30/38), the absent token expiry (CWE-613, ~74-75) and the cookie missing Secure and SameSite (CWE-614, ~86). Also note finding 03 is a STORED XSS in comments (the cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443 at 02:18:47), not reflected, even though your evidence line was right. The chain is too compressed though; you collapsed it to four hops and dropped the stored XSS (02:18:47) and open redirect (02:21:13) hops that sit between auth bypass and file read, so the in-order reconciliation is incomplete. Your CVSS strings are complete vectors but they sit bare in a table with no justifying sentence each, and the SQLi vector should be AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1, not A:H, because the login bypass does not hit availability. You also missed the senior insight that the forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service, which is a scope change to S:C. Your impact section is the highlight here: 312 records, an average-balance assumption stated openly, about 55M NGN of direct exposure and the BoltCash launch tie are all reasoned rather than asserted. D3: This is your best deliverable. The executive summary lands on 312 customer records and the BoltCash risk, the threat model is present, the findings table ties to evidence, and you restated the disproved decoy correctly. Most importantly your remediation table is genuinely ordered by Risk Reduction per Hour and effort, XXE first because it is low effort, MD5 last because it is very high effort, which is the effort-to-risk reasoning the brief asks for rather than blind CVSS ordering. Both detection stopgaps are deployable with exact patterns, target fields and false-positive rates (<0.1% for the XXE WAF rule, <1% for the SQLi/traversal SIEM alert). To push this higher, name the earliest-break fix explicitly: the SQLi at login is the root entry, so the prepared-statement fix is the single hop that breaks the whole chain. D4: You answered all four prompts in your own voice with a clear owned decision, declined the journalist cleanly, refused to bury the console-timeline evidence, and made breach notification the non-negotiable action. ISC2 Canon 1 is cited by number and is load-bearing in your argument. The one real slip is the NDPA section: the 72-hour duty to notify the NDPC is Section 40, and Section 41 covers notifying affected data subjects on high risk, not Section 30, so cite those and tie them to the 312 customers. The single most important fix: catalogue all ten findings with quoted lines and reconcile every chain hop in order, because a partial catalogue and a compressed chain are what separate this from a high-70s report.

You submitted a single PDF containing D4, your ethics stance, and on its own terms it is a strong, mature piece of work. You answer all four prompts in a clearly anchored first-person voice: you turn down the journalist's off-the-record DM and explain why off the record is a liability rather than a favour in a live incident, you define narrowly what you will and will not put in writing, you commit to presenting the decommissioning timeline factually to the security authority rather than handing it selectively to anyone who would use it as a shield or a weapon, and you name the action you take regardless of internal preference. On the NDPA you correctly identify Sankofa as data controller, the duty to notify the regulator within the statutory window, and the duty to notify affected data subjects where the breach is high risk, anchored to the 312 customers and your own decode of the exfil. The one factual slip is that you name NITDA as the notifying authority when under the NDPA 2023 the supervisory authority is the NDPC; the obligations themselves are right, so this cost you only a small deduction rather than the row. Where I have to be honest with you is that this submission contained only D4. D1 the findings, D2 the exploit chain and CVSS, and D3 the written report were not present at your link, so each of those three deliverables scored zero, and that is why your overall number is low despite the quality of the ethics page. Nothing about the missing work reflects on the D4 you wrote; it simply was not there to grade. The single most important next step is to submit D1, D2, and D3, since those three carry 105 of the 120 marks and are the bulk of what this capstone is testing.

D1 is a clean but incomplete catalogue. You caught seven of the ten findings and every one you listed carries the right class and CWE with a quoted line: SQLi A03/CWE-89 at login.php 64-67, unsalted MD5 A02/CWE-916 at line 66, JWT alg:none A07/CWE-347 at 48-50, the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 A02/CWE-798 at 30/38, XXE A05/CWE-611, the stored XSS A03/CWE-79 at 02:18:47, and the cookie missing Secure and SameSite A05/CWE-614. What costs you is three missing findings: no token expiry CWE-613 around lines 74-75, path traversal CWE-22 from the files/?path=/etc/passwd capture at 02:24:02, and the open redirect CWE-601 from ?next= at 02:21:13. Your detection stopgaps are generic WAF and logging with no exact log field and no false-positive rate. D4: You cite ISC2 Canon I by number in a load-bearing way, which is correct, but the piece is about 285 words and under the 300 floor, you reference the NDPA without the section, where you needed section 40 (notify NDPC within 72 hours) and section 41 (notify data subjects on high risk) tied to the 312 customers, and the four prompts (the journalist, what you put in writing, the colleague evidence, the one action regardless of the manager) are not all clearly answered in your own voice. You catalogued nine of the ten findings with correct OWASP and CWE mappings and, importantly, you quoted the actual evidence line for most of them: the concatenated login query for the SQLi (A03/CWE-89), the MD5('...') call for unsalted hashing (A02/CWE-916), the 'if (alg === none) return payload' branch for the JWT bypass (A07/CWE-347), the literal 'sankofa-legacy-admin-2019' for the hardcoded secret (CWE-798), the setcookie line for the missing Secure/SameSite flags (CWE-614), and the file:///etc/passwd entity for the XXE. The one finding you missed is the open redirect on ?next= (CWE-601, visible at capture 02:21:13), and your stored XSS row cites only the POST endpoint without the cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443 that proves exploitation, so that finding earns partial. Your PoCs are good, the assembled alg:none token, the SQLi query, the path-traversal request and the exfil request are all verbatim and usable, but the chain is incomplete and out of order: you dropped the stored-XSS hop at 02:18:47 and the open-redirect hop at 02:21:13 entirely, and you placed the 312-row exfil at 02:16:04 as Stage 5 after the 02:24:02 file read, which breaks the timeline. The detection stopgaps are genuinely strong: a WAF rule on the legacy_admin_jwt cookie prefix eyJhbGciOiJub25lI with a 0.00% false-positive rationale, and a SIEM rule on uri_path /files/ with a sub-0.50% rate, both with exact fields. The row that caps D3 is remediation ordering: you explicitly ordered by CVSS severity and even wrote that the sequence 'should follow CVSS scoring rather than effort assessment', which is the opposite of what the brief asked, remediation should be ordered by effort-to-risk so quick high-impact fixes land first. Your CVSS vectors are complete and justified, and the S:C scope change on alg:none with the internal-API reasoning is the senior insight we wanted, but you scored SQL injection 9.8 with A:H; the auth bypass does not touch availability, so it is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1. Your chain in D2 is only four hops and misses the recon (02:14:08), the failed guess (02:14:55), the stored XSS (02:18:47), and the open redirect (02:21:13), and you mislabelled the 02:16:04 bulk PII pull as a scouting timestamp; reconcile every hop to its own capture line next time. The impact math is good and honest: 312 customers, a transparent 20-record sample average, and roughly 63M NGN projected with the BoltCash launch tie-in, and you showed your assumptions rather than dropping a bare number. D3 is excellent and carries the report. The exec summary lands on customers and naira, the threat model pulls in the /api/v1/internal scope comment, the earliest-break fix (block /legacy-admin/ at the edge) is right, and crucially your remediation table is ordered by effort versus risk reduction with hours and percentages rather than by CVSS, which is the discipline most reports miss. D4 answers all four prompts in a clear owned voice anchored to your own line-42 finding, cites ISC2 Canon I by number and load-bearing, and ties the breach to the 312 customers, but your NDPA section is wrong: the 72-hour NDPC notification duty is section 40 and the data-subject notification on high risk is section 41, not section 31. The single most important fix: complete your finding catalogue and your exploit chain so the two missing findings (stored XSS and the hardcoded secret) and every capture timestamp are accounted for, and correct the SQLi vector to A:N.

name: Abayomi Kehinde
feedback: D1 is a strong, evidence-led catalogue. You found all ten core findings plus two defensible extras (CSRF, role-from-JWT), and every row carries a quoted source line or a capture timestamp, which is exactly the standard. SQL injection at lines 64-67, alg:none at 48-50, the hardcoded sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 secret at line 30, the no-exp comment at 74-75, the stored XSS beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443 at 02:18:47, and the path traversal returning root:x:0:0 at 02:24:02 are all nailed. Two CWE choices drift (MD5 is fine as CWE-327 even though CWE-916 is the cleaner fit, and you put alg:none under A03 when it is really A07 auth failure), but the evidence lines are right so I credited them. Where D1 loses ground is the decoy. You disproved iat, and your reasoning that iat is inert and the real bug is the missing exp is internally sound, but iat was not the designated safe construct. The intended decoy is the HS256 verify branch using hash_equals(), which is constant-time and genuinely sound, so the tempting move was to flag it and the proof was to show the timing-safe comparison defeats that. You did not engage that construct, so that row stays low. To be clear, this is a miss and not fabrication; you never invented an exploit or rated a safe thing Critical, which is why there is no penalty. D2 is your weakest deliverable. The hops you wrote up (SQLi at 02:15:31, session at 02:15:33, the 312-row pull at 02:16:04, then the export) are reconciled verbatim to the capture and your PoC strings match the artefact. The problem is the chain stops short: you dropped the stored XSS at 02:18:47, the open redirect at 02:21:13, and the file read at 02:24:02 out of the D2 narrative entirely, and you never anchored the recon at 02:14:08 or the failed guess at 02:14:55. A full exploit chain has to walk every hop in order, so half the chain points are gone. Your SQLi CVSS vector is complete and well justified, but you set A:H when the bypass does not touch availability; the correct vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N for about 9.1, not 9.8. You did capture the scope change on the export as S:C, which is the senior insight, good. The impact section is genuinely excellent: 312 customers, the ₦6,400 to ₦950,000 range, the ₦200,000 average stated as an assumption, ₦62.4M total, and the BoltCash six-week clock all land. D3 is the standout. The executive summary is jargon-free and ends on the customers-and-naira headline, the threat model names the external actor and the shared /api/v1/internal service, all twelve findings are tied to evidence, and crucially your remediation table is ordered by effort-to-risk and not by CVSS, with the 2-hour SQL parameterisation first and 2-day MD5 rehashing last, defended as highest risk reduction per hour. Your two stopgaps give exact ModSecurity rules on ARGS:username and ARGS:path with a stated sub-1 percent false-positive rate and a reason. The only soft spot in D3 is repeating the iat decoy instead of the hash_equals one. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, cites ISC2 Canon I and Canon IV by number, anchors the decision to the SQLi you found at lines 64-67 and the 312 rows you counted yourself, and triggers the NDPA breach duty with the 72-hour NDPC clock and the high-risk data-subject notification. The one gap is that you named the duties but not the sections, so cite section 40 for the 72-hour NDPC notification and section 41 for notifying the 312 affected data subjects. The single most important fix is to complete the D2 exploit chain so it walks every captured hop in order from recon at 02:14:08 through the file read at 02:24:02, because a half-chain undersells an intrusion you otherwise reconstructed very well.

feedback: D1 is excellent and is the high point of this submission. You catalogued all ten of the planted findings with quoted evidence, correct OWASP categories, and CWE IDs, and you went past the minimum with the role-trust and username-enumeration extras. SQL injection (A03/CWE-89) carries the concatenated MD5 login line, the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (A02/CWE-798), alg:none (A07), no exp/nbf (CWE-613), stored XSS with the 185.220.101.9:8443 cookie beacon, XXE file:///etc/passwd, path traversal, open redirect, and the missing Secure/SameSite cookie are all here and proved. Your CWE-327 for MD5 and CWE-345 for alg:none are defensible class variants, so they keep full credit. The decoy is handled correctly: you named hash_equals and proved it safe at the mechanism level as a constant-time comparison rather than inventing an exploit, which is exactly right. D2 is the weakest deliverable. Your CVSS table is mostly complete with justifications, but the SQLi vector should be AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N for about 9.1, not A:H for 9.8, because an auth bypass does not degrade availability. The bigger gap is the chain itself: you compressed it to five hops and dropped the stored XSS hop at 02:18:47 and the open redirect hop at 02:21:13 even though you found both in D1, so the timeline does not fully reconcile to the captures. You also missed the senior insight that a forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service, which is a scope change to S:C. Your ₦78M impact with a stated ₦250k average assumption is acceptable because you showed your working, though balances actually run up to roughly 950k. D3 is very strong: the executive summary lands on a customers-and-naira headline, the threat model names the external attacker and IP, the decoy is disproved correctly, the earliest-break fix is correctly identified as the SQL injection, your remediation is ordered explicitly by risk reduction per engineering effort rather than CVSS, and both detection stopgaps give an exact log field and a false-positive rationale. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, cites ISC2 Canon I and Canon II load-bearingly, and anchors to your 312-record finding, but you cited the NDPA 2023 only by name. The single most important fix is to cite the NDPA by section in D4, section 40 for the 72-hour NDPC notification and section 41 for notifying the 312 affected data subjects, and to reconcile every chain hop in D2 back to its capture timestamp.

D1: This is a genuinely strong catalogue. You quoted the login concatenation for SQL injection (A03/CWE-89), the MD5 hashing line, the alg:none skip branch, the missing exp/nbf for no token expiry (CWE-613), the open redirect on next, the setcookie without Secure (CWE-614), the XXE ENTITY file:///etc/passwd line, and the files/?path=/etc/passwd traversal. Nine of the ten real findings are present with evidence, which is well above a partial catalogue. Two real problems hold the row back. The hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 should be its own finding as A05/CWE-798, not folded into a vague weak-and-guessable note, and you missed the stored-XSS cookie beacon at 02:18:47 to 185.220.101.9:8443 that proves exfiltration. The decoy is also inverted. The safe construct is the HS256 verify branch that uses hash_equals, which is constant-time and sound, so the right move is to name it, show it is safe at the mechanism level, and explain that the real bugs are alg:none and the hardcoded secret. You instead labeled JWT-HS256-is-secure as FALSE and called it insecure, which disproves the safe construct rather than proving it safe, so that part earns nothing. D2: The chain is mostly in the right order and several hops carry verbatim PoCs (admin' OR '1'='1, the next redirect, the path traversal, the XXE entity), but the stored-XSS hop has no payload, the SQLi CVSS uses A:H when the bypass does not touch availability so it should be AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at roughly 9.1, and the impact is bare. You wrote 312 customers but gave no naira, no balances up to about 950k summing to tens of millions, no BoltCash tie-in, and no stated assumptions, which is most of the impact row. D3: The executive summary ends on a generic call to action rather than the customers-and-naira headline a board needs, only five findings carry evidence here, the decoy is restated incorrectly, no earliest-break fix is named, the detection stopgaps give patterns and a Low false-positive note but no exact log field, and the remediation is explicitly ordered by CVSS severity rather than by effort-to-risk, which caps that row at half. D4: You answer all four prompts in your own voice, cite ISC2 Canon II by number in a load-bearing way, and anchor to the 312 records, but you name the NDPA only in general and never cite section 40 for the 72-hour NDPC notification or section 41 for notifying the 312 data subjects, so that row is empty. I have to be straight with you about the most serious issue. The SSRF to 169.254.169.254 metadata with IAM credentials and full infrastructure compromise does not exist in this pack, there is no capture line for it, and it drove your headline CVSS 9.9. Inventing an exploit and evidence is fabrication, so that finding scores zero and a five-point penalty applies. I looked hard for a way to round this up because your real catalogue is strong, but the fabricated SSRF, the inverted decoy, and the missing impact figures will not support a higher mark. The single most important fix is to stop inventing findings: grade only what the evidence proves, get the decoy right by proving the hash_equals branch safe, and quantify impact in naira tied to the 312 BoltCash customers.

name: Shedrach Nohense
feedback: D1 is a strong, well evidenced catalogue. You captured nine of the ten real findings with correct CWE and a quoted line each, F-01 SQLi (CWE-89, capture 02:15:31), F-02 unsalted MD5 (CWE-916), F-03 alg:none (CWE-347, Token 2), F-04 no expiry (CWE-613), F-05 cookie no Secure (CWE-614), F-06 path traversal (CWE-22, 02:24:02), F-07 stored XSS (CWE-79, 02:18:47), F-08 XXE (CWE-611) and F-09 hardcoded secret (CWE-321). The one place D1 fell down is the decoy. You labelled the open redirect as the false positive, but the open redirect is a real finding (capture 02:21:13 shows the 302 to 185.220.101.9:8443, A01/CWE-601), and the actual safe construct you were meant to disprove is the HS256 verify branch using hash_equals(), which is constant time and therefore sound, the real auth bugs being alg:none and the hardcoded secret. That single mistake cost you both the decoy row and the open redirect as a tenth finding. D2 is the best part of the submission. The timeline reconstructs recon, SQLi at 02:15:31, the 312 row pull at 02:16:04, stored XSS at 02:18:47, XXE at 02:23:41 and path traversal at 02:24:02, each tied to a capture line, and your verbatim PoCs (the admin' OR '1'='1 payload, the decoded alg:none token, the XXE body, the /files/?path=/etc/passwd request) are exactly what we want to see. Two notes, you dropped the open redirect hop from the chain because you treated it as a decoy, and on F-01 you scored A:H for 9.8 when the login bypass does not touch availability, so the correct vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1. Your BoltCash chain row did capture the senior insight with S:C reaching /api/v1/internal, which is good. The impact figure of about 132 million naira scaled from the 20 row sample average with the assumption stated is well argued. D3 reads cleanly, the exec summary lands on 312 customers and the naira headline and the 72 hour NDPC duty, the STRIDE model maps to evidence, and your two detection stopgaps name exact fields and justified false positive rates (under 0.5 percent for the WAF rule, about 2 percent for the SIEM query). The disproved finding section repeats the open redirect error and so scores nothing there, and your remediation order is argued by entry path rather than strictly by effort to risk, which is why that row is not full, the 30 minute XXE fix sitting last is the tell. D4 is excellent and full marks, all four prompts are answered in your own voice, you cite ISC2 Canon 1 by number load bearing, and you tie NDPA Section 40 and the 72 hour clock directly to the 312 customers. The single most important fix is to learn the decoy, prove the hash_equals branch safe at the mechanism level and keep the open redirect as a genuine finding, that one correction would have lifted both D1 and D3.

name: Abdurrahman Bala Bako
feedback: D1 is the strongest part of this submission. You catalogued all ten vulnerabilities plus the decoy, and almost every finding carries a quoted code line or a capture timestamp, which is exactly what earns full credit. SQL injection in 01-legacy-admin-login.php is nailed with the string-concat WHERE clause and the admin' OR '1'='1 payload tied to 02:15:31, stored XSS is tied to the cookie beacon at 02:18:47, path traversal shows the root:x:0:0 response at 02:24:02, and the XXE entity is quoted. A few CWE numbers drifted, MD5 as CWE-327 rather than CWE-916, alg:none as CWE-345 rather than CWE-347, and the cookie flags as CWE-1004 rather than CWE-614, and XXE was filed under A03 rather than A05, all of which are defensible class variants so I did not punish them hard. Your decoy handling is correct and the reason I held D1 high: you named hash_equals as the tempting safe construct, proved it safe because constant-time comparison defeats timing attacks, and correctly kept alg:none as a real bug rather than calling it the decoy, which is the trap many candidates fall into. D2 reconciles the chain hop by hop with timestamps and verbatim payloads, which is good, but the CVSS work let you down on the flagship finding. You scored SQL injection 10.0 with S:C and A:H, and the defensible vector here is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at roughly 9.1, because an auth bypass does not touch availability and does not change scope at that hop, so revisit A:N and S:U there. Your impact section names 312 customers and the 6,400 to 950,000 NGN balance range and honestly states that no live testing was done, but you stopped short of summing the exposure into a tens-of-millions naira figure and you never connected it to BoltCash or to the forged super_admin token reaching the shared /api/v1/internal service, which is the senior scope-change insight that would have lifted this row. D3 reads cleanly, ties findings to artefacts, states the decoy correctly, and names SQL injection as the single earliest-break fix, all of which I credited. Two things held it back: your remediation is ordered by risk-reduction and impact rather than by effort-to-risk, which is the ordering the brief asked for, and your two detection stopgaps name log patterns but give no false-positive rates, so an operator cannot judge the noise, add an exact field and an FP estimate for each. D4 is in a strong personal voice and is anchored to your own findings, but it only answers two of the four prompts cleanly, the what-goes-in-writing prompt and the one-non-negotiable-action prompt are not clearly resolved, you cite ISC2 Canon I and II by number which is good, but you never name the NDPA 2023 breach duty, so add section 40 for the 72-hour NDPC notification and section 41 for notifying the 312 affected data subjects on high risk. No fabrication was present, every evidence line traces to the pack. The single most important fix is to correct the SQL injection CVSS vector to S:U and A:N around 9.1 and to justify each metric in one sentence, because a wrong score on your top finding undermines the whole risk story.

name: Amugo Grace Nene
feedback: D1 is a strong catalogue. You caught nine of the ten real findings with quoted evidence lines, including the SQLi at lines 61 to 64 with the 02:15:31 admin' OR '1'='1 capture, the unsalted MD5 at line 63, the alg none token (Token 2), the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 at line 30, the missing expiry on Token 1, the stored XSS at 02:18:47, the path traversal at 02:24:02, the open redirect at 02:21:13, and the cookie Secure flag at line 80. The one real miss is the XXE. Your Finding 10 reads 04-import-xxe.xml as a mere syntax error and tags it CWE-112, when the actual issue is an XML external entity injection (A05, CWE-611) where the SYSTEM declaration pulls file:///etc/passwd, so that finding lost most of its credit. Your decoy work is correct and well argued, you named the b64url helpers, gave the not exploitable verdict, and proved it at the mechanism level rather than just asserting it, and you correctly treated alg none as a real bug and not the decoy. D2 chains cleanly with genuinely verbatim proof of concept blocks, full request and response and notes for each hop, but you compressed the eight observable events into four hops and left the recon, the failed guess, the XSS, and the open redirect out of the reconciled sequence, which cost you on the chain row. On CVSS your vectors are complete and you wrote a justifying sentence, which is what earns full marks, but you scored SQL injection as S:C for a base of 10.0 when SQLi on its own is S:U at roughly 9.1, the scope change really belongs to the forged super_admin token reaching the shared /api/v1/internal service, so apply that S:C where it is earned. Your impact figure is good because you showed the assumption, an average of about 192,660 naira across the viewable rows applied to 312 customers for about 60.1 million naira tied to the BoltCash launch in six weeks, that reasoning is exactly what we want over a bare number. D3 is the standout. The executive summary is jargon free and lands on the 312 customers and 60.1 million naira headline, the threat model names the shared microservice trust, the earliest break is correct (kill alg none at stage two), and your remediation table is genuinely ordered by effort to risk with hour estimates and a column explaining why each rank beats a higher CVSS target, which is the hard part most people get wrong. Your two detection stopgaps give exact fields, the header cookie and authorization regex and the POST_BODY login rule, each with a stated false positive rate and a reason. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, cites ISC2 Canon I load bearing, anchors to your own 312 ledger finding, and names NDPA Section 40 with the 72 hour NDPC duty, though Section 40 is the regulator notification and Section 41 is the duty to notify the 312 affected data subjects on high risk, so split those two next time. The single most important fix is to recognise the XXE in 04-import-xxe.xml as an external entity read of /etc/passwd rather than a parsing syntax error, because that is a substantial finding you reported as noise.

name: STEPHEN ADEYEMI ADEJINMI
feedback: On D1 this is a near-complete catalogue and it is excellent work.
