Your scope-change reasoning to the shared /api/v1/internal service is the senior insight the key rewards, and your impact section states its assumptions (mean of the sample, the CUST-0137 outlier handling, the NGN 31M to 53M floor and ceiling against 312 accounts) instead of throwing out a bare number. The main deduction on D2 is the SQLi vector: you scored 10.0 with A:H, but the login bypass does not hit availability, so the defensible answer is A:N giving roughly 9.1, and your UNION-locks-the-table justification is a reach. D3 is comprehensive and well structured. The executive summary is jargon-free and lands on the customers-and-naira headline, the threat model is concrete (Tor exit node, 17-minute deliberate session), findings are tied to quoted evidence, the decoy is disproved cleanly, the earliest-break fix is correctly the parameterised query at lines 52-55, and crucially your remediation table is ordered by effort-to-risk not CVSS severity, you rank the 6.1 open redirect above the 8.5 XXE on a per-engineering-hour basis and say so explicitly, which is exactly what the row asks for. Your two detection stopgaps name the exact log field and a defended false-positive rate. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, anchors to your own findings (05-exfil-sample.csv matched to the 02:16:04 312-row response), and cites ISC2 Canon I and Canon II by number and load-bearing. The one gap that holds D4 back is the NDPA citation: you name the 2023 breach duty and describe both the regulator notification and the high-risk data-subject notification, but you cite a statutory window in prose rather than the sections by number, so add NDPA 2023 section 40 (notify the NDPC within 72 hours) and section 41 (notify data subjects on high risk) to make it precise. No fabrication anywhere, every figure traces to the exfil sample with assumptions stated, which is why this scores high. The single most important fix is to drop the SQLi vector to A:N (about 9.1) and stop assigning A:H where the exploit does not affect availability.

name: Genius Franklyn
feedback: D1 is a model catalogue. You captured all ten canonical findings and then some, each row carrying the OWASP class, the right CWE, and a quoted evidence line: SQLi at login.php 64-67 with the admin' OR '1'='1 bypass at 02:15:31, unsalted MD5 (CWE-916) at line 66, alg:none (CWE-347) at 48-50 proven by Token 2, the hard-coded sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 secret (CWE-798) at line 30, no exp (CWE-613), stored XSS with the cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443 at 02:18:47, XXE in 04-import-xxe.xml, path traversal at 02:24:02 returning root:x:0:0, open redirect at 02:21:13, and the insecure cookie at line 86. The decoy is handled exactly right: you named the hand-rolled JWT block as the tempting target, proved the HS256 branch sound at the mechanism level because hash_equals is constant-time, and correctly kept alg:none as a real vulnerability rather than mislabeling it the decoy. That is full marks. One small blemish: the finding-12 table header reads 84,210-row while your prose and every other artefact says 312, so fix that typo before it confuses a reader. D2 reconstructs the chain cleanly in four hops, each reconciled to a capture line with verbatim proof, and you landed the senior insight that matters, scoring the SQLi S:C because the forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service. Your CVSS vectors are complete and each carries a justifying sentence, and the impact section quantifies 312 customers with balances from roughly 6,400 to 950,000 naira aggregating to tens of millions, stating the representativeness assumption and tying it to the BoltCash launch in six weeks. The only thing keeping D2 from full is that you compressed recon (02:14:08) and the failed guess (02:14:55) out of the hop sequence and folded open redirect and XSS into side rows rather than placing every hop in strict order, so the chain reads as four hops instead of the fuller walk. D3 is close to complete. The executive summary is genuinely jargon-free and ends on the customers-and-naira headline, the threat model frames a deliberate human under seventeen minutes, the findings tie to evidence, the decoy is disproved correctly, and crucially your remediation table is ordered by risk reduction per hour of effort and you say so explicitly, ranking the SQLi fix first because it breaks the chain at step one for four to eight hours of work. Both detection stopgaps give exact SIEM and WAF field patterns with a stated false-positive rate, which is what the row asks for. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, declines the journalist, keeps written reporting narrow to Amaka with no names, treats the timeline as evidence that goes up the channel untouched, and commits to notifying the NDPC regardless of the manager, anchored to the 312 records. You cite ISC2 Canon II and Canon I by number and load-bearing. The one gap that cost you in D4 is that you reference the NDPA 2023 breach duty as a legal clock running but never name the section, so add section 40 for the 72-hour NDPC notification and section 41 for notifying the 312 data subjects on high risk. Most important fix: name the NDPA sections by number in D4 and tighten the 84,210 typo in D1, and this already-excellent capstone is airtight.

name: Kipngeno Kendrick
missingPieces: Stored XSS (capture 02:18:47, CWE-79) is not catalogued as a numbered finding in D1; it appears only as Hop 5 in D2. SQLi CVSS in D2 uses A:H (9.8) where A:N (~9.1) is correct. Senior scope-change insight (forged super_admin token reaching the shared /api/v1/internal service, S:C) is not raised.
feedback: D1 is a strong, evidence-led catalogue. You quote the actual source lines for SQLi (login.php:47, the MD5 string-concat query), alg:none (login.php:38-42 with the literal if block), the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019, the no-expiry jwt_issue call, open redirect, XXE and path traversal at 02:24:02 returning root:x:0:0, and every one carries an OWASP class and a CWE. CWE-321 for the hardcoded secret and A02 for the cookie flags are defensible variants, so I credited them. The one real gap is stored XSS: the cookie-beacon payload at 02:18:47 is one of the ten and it never appears as a numbered finding in D1, it only surfaces as Hop 5 in D2, so that finding lost its share here. Your decoy work is exactly right, you name the b64url helpers, prove at the mechanism level that they only do URL-safe encoding while the real signing is delegated to native hash_hmac, and you correctly keep alg:none on the real-bug side rather than mislabelling it the decoy. D2 is excellent: all seven hops are in order and each is reconciled to a verbatim capture line with the real PoC, the admin' OR '1'='1 body, the 312-row pull at 02:16:04, the script fetch beacon, the ?next= redirect and the XXE DOCTYPE. Your CVSS vectors are complete strings, but the justifications are thin one-liners and your SQLi vector uses A:H giving 9.8 when the bypass does not touch availability, so the correct vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1. The impact section is the highlight: 312 customers, a stated 20-row sample average of about 202k NGN extrapolated to roughly 63M aggregate, clearly labelled funds-at-risk rather than loss, plus the NDPA fine ceiling and the BoltCash six-week window, all assumptions stated and traced to the exfil sample, so no fabrication. D3 is near-complete and well aimed at Bayo: jargon-free summary ending on customers and naira, a threat model, findings tied to line citations, the decoy disproved correctly, and crucially a remediation table explicitly ordered by risk-reduction-per-hour rather than CVSS, with effort notes like one function call and three lines, which is exactly the ask. Your two detection stopgaps both name an exact field and a false-positive rate, the WAF/SIEM SQLi rule on http.request.body.content and the alg:none cookie-prefix rule eyJhbGciOiJub25lIi, both well reasoned. The only slip in D3 is calling the app a Django panel when login.php is plainly PHP. D4 is a clean 15: all four prompts answered in your own voice, ISC2 Canon 3 cited by number and load-bearing, NDPA 2023 Sections 40 and 41 named and tied to the 312 customers and their PII, and the timeline-evidence reasoning about Ngozi's objection is genuinely thoughtful. The single most important fix is to catalogue every one of the ten findings in D1 itself, the missing stored XSS cost you there, and to correct the SQLi CVSS to A:N (9.1) so your severities match the evidence.

name: TAMERA OBIAGERI OKAFOR
missingPieces: D2 SQL injection CVSS uses A:H giving 9.8; the auth bypass does not affect availability so the correct vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1. feedback: D1 is a near-complete catalogue and the strongest part of this submission. You found all ten canonical vulnerabilities, each with a quoted source line or capture line and a correct or defensible OWASP plus CWE pairing: the SQL injection at lines 65 to 66 with the concatenated WHERE clause, the alg:none acceptance with Token 2, the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 at line 30, the missing exp claim on Tokens 1 and 3, unsalted MD5, the XXE SYSTEM file read, path traversal at 02:24:02 returning root:x:0:0, the stored XSS cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9 at 02:18:47, the open redirect at 02:21:13, and the cookie missing Secure and SameSite. One small label slip: you tagged path traversal as A02 Broken Access Control when Broken Access Control is A01, but the CWE-22 and the evidence line are right so it keeps credit. You also nailed the decoy by naming hash_equals at line 53, ruling it not exploitable, and proving it at the mechanism level as constant-time comparison while correctly pointing to alg:none as the real bug. D2 is strong. The chain runs in order with each hop reconciled to a timestamp, the PoC payloads are verbatim, and the scope-change insight is captured in the paragraph about JWT forgery reaching dependent services that trust the token. The one real error is the SQL injection CVSS: you used A:H to reach 9.8, but the authentication bypass does not impair availability, so the vector should be AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N for about 9.1. Your impact work is exactly what was wanted, with the 20-row sample averaged to about 202,011.60 naira, extrapolated to 312 customers for 63,027,619 naira, the assumption stated plainly, and the BoltCash launch tied in. D3 is polished: the executive summary is jargon-free and ends on the customers-and-naira headline, the threat model names the external attacker and the shared JWT trust, the decoy is restated correctly, the chain ends on the earliest-break SQLi fix, the remediation table is genuinely ordered by risk reduction per hour with effort estimates rather than raw severity, and both detection stopgaps give a concrete field and a false-positive rate. The only blemish is that the CVSS lines inside the F1 to F7 bodies are left as the empty template string, though you do supply the full vectors in the table that follows. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, cites ISC2 canon I by number as load-bearing, names NDPA section 40 tied to the breached customers, and anchors to your own findings; watch the slip where you wrote 313 customers instead of 312. Nothing here is fabricated; every figure and line traces to the evidence pack. This is excellent, near-complete work. The single most important fix is to correct the SQL injection availability metric to A:N so the vector and the score reflect that an auth bypass does not take the service down.

name: Abdullateef Oladejo
feedback: D1 is strong and evidence-led, with SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, no expiry, stored XSS, XXE, path traversal, open redirect, and the cookie flag all tied to source lines or capture times. The main D1 gap is the missing hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 as its own finding, and the cookie issue should mention both Secure and SameSite. D1 also deserves real credit for correctly disproving the hand-rolled HS256 hash_equals branch and the b64url helpers as the decoy. The D3 exploit-chain section is good, although the earliest break should be reasoned against the whole chain and not only the backend token path. D4 answers the ethical scenario in an owned voice and uses ISC2 Canons II and III meaningfully. It should cite the NDPA breach duties by the expected sections, especially section 40 for notifying the NDPC within 72 hours and section 41 for affected data subjects, tied to the 312 customers. The single most important fix is to include the hardcoded JWT secret and the full chronological D2 chain instead of leaving those as implied context.

name: Prince Ubebe

name: Anthony Odey
feedback: D1 has good breadth and correctly identifies the main SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, missing expiry, weak JWT secret, XXE, stored XSS, path traversal, open redirect, and mass data exposure themes. It loses decoy credit because it selects the reflected login error as the disproved issue, while the required safe construct is the b64url helpers and especially the HS256 hash_equals branch. name: ADEOBA ADEDOTUN TAIWO
feedback: D1 is excellent: it captures the ten answer-key findings and more, ties them to source lines or capture evidence, separates cookie flags from the XSS discussion, and gives a precise decoy proof for b64url encoding and hash_equals. name: Michael Ted Ndeda Kibanda

name: Nada maach
feedback: D1 is the main weakness because it is written as an intrusion reconstruction timeline rather than the required findings catalogue. It proves SQL injection, bulk access, stored XSS, open redirect, and path traversal, but it does not catalogue MD5 password hashing, alg:none, the hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, XXE, cookie flags, or the actual hash_equals decoy. name: Obioma Felicity Uzoh
feedback: D1 identifies several important findings, including SQL injection, alg:none, MD5, missing token expiry, cookie flags, open redirect, and the correct hash_equals decoy. It misses the hardcoded JWT secret as a full substantive finding, and it does not include stored XSS, XXE, or path traversal in the catalogue, which costs a lot under the D1 row. D1 also relies on figure placeholders rather than quoting all the evidence directly in the text, so the reader has less proof than the rubric asks for. The PoC slots are mostly empty placeholders, so even though the narrative is useful it does not fully meet the verbatim artefact requirement. It lacks a proper substantiated findings section, does not restate the exploit chain in enough detail, and only covers four remediation priorities. The single most important fix is to complete the D1 catalogue and D3 findings section rather than leaving critical rows to implication or figures.

name: Aladeloye Joshua
feedback: D1 covers the core authentication and access-control findings well, including SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, no expiry, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, cookie flags, and broken access control on users.php. It loses significant D1 credit because the required decoy is not the XSS cookie-theft branch, it is the b64url helpers and HS256 hash_equals comparison. The stored XSS should have been listed as a real finding with evidence rather than placed in the decoy row, even if the specific document.cookie theft of an HttpOnly cookie would fail. D2 provides a useful eight-hop chain and a strong impact discussion with 312 records and a roughly NGN 63.5m estimate, with the right caveat that the naira figure is extrapolated. It does not include the initial recon and failed login as required hops, and the forged JWT step is not reconciled to a capture line because it is code and token evidence rather than an observed request. D2's CVSS vectors are mostly complete, although several omit the CVSS:3.1 prefix and the XSS impact is reduced because of the decoy framing. D3 is persuasive at the executive level, with a clear threat model, estimated balance exposure, and remediation ordered by risk reduction per hour. It loses credit for relying on D1 for evidence instead of tying findings to evidence in the report itself, for carrying forward the wrong decoy, and for giving detection stopgaps without false-positive rates. D4 has a strong disclosure stance and uses ISC2 Canons I, II, and III well, plus it correctly describes the 72-hour NDPC and affected-customer notification duties in substance. It does not answer the personal journalist prompt, the internal writing prompt, or the colleague-evidence pressure as directly as required, and it does not cite NDPA section 40 or 41 by number. The single most important fix is to replace the XSS-cookie decoy with the actual hash_equals decoy and make stored XSS a normal finding.

name: Sellwane Matsheka
feedback: D1 is careful and evidence-based, and it gets strong credit for SQL injection, alg:none, missing expiry, XXE, path traversal, stored XSS, open redirect, cookie flags, and MD5. The major D1 problem is that the hardcoded JWT secret is treated as the decoy, when the answer key requires it as a real finding. The actual decoy should have been the b64url helpers and the HS256 hash_equals comparison, not the sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 secret. D2 is strong: it reconstructs the chain with useful PoCs, distinguishes captured activity from code-only JWT proof, and gives a good customer and naira impact estimate. It loses some D2 credit because the recon and failed-login steps are not formal hops and because the hardcoded secret is not scored as a real JWT forgery path. D3 is well written, business-facing, and includes a clear customers-and-naira headline, a good threat model, a sensible chain explanation, and concrete detection stopgaps with false-positive expectations. D3 again loses credit for the wrong decoy and for de-prioritizing the hardcoded secret as though rotating it would not matter. D4 is excellent in tone and judgment: it refuses the journalist, defines what goes in writing, preserves colleague-related timeline evidence, and ties the NDPA section 40 duty to 312 customers. It should also cite section 41 for direct affected-customer notification, but the substance is present. The single most important fix is to stop treating the hardcoded JWT secret as a decoy and catalogue it as a real high-impact finding.

name: Oriaku Chioma Angela
flagReason: Fabricated business-impact range in D3: ₦200M to ₦400M does not trace to the exfil sample.
feedback: D1 is broad and mostly accurate, with SQL injection, alg:none, MD5, missing expiry, hardcoded secret, open redirect, cookie flags, users.php exposure, stored XSS, path traversal, and XXE all present with evidence. It gets only partial decoy credit because it correctly dismisses b64url_decode as only encoding conversion, but it does not address the HS256 hash_equals branch that the answer key specifically expects. name: Jedidah Umaru
feedback: D1 has a concise catalogue with several correct core findings: SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, no expiry, open redirect, cookie flags, path traversal, XXE, and users.php data exposure. It misses stored XSS as a real finding, and the chosen decoy, an empty comments POST, is not the required safe construct. The required decoy is the b64url helpers and especially the HS256 hash_equals comparison. It should cite NDPA sections 40 and 41 by number and anchor the ISC2 canons a little more deeply, but the ethical direction is right. I looked for a defensible reason to push this higher, but the missing stored XSS, wrong decoy, and partial D2 and D3 coverage keep it in this band. The single most important fix is to add the stored XSS finding and replace the empty-comment decoy with the hash_equals decoy.

name: Utibe Owoabasi Obot
flagReason: Fabricated SSRF and AWS metadata evidence not present in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 has some good work, especially SQL injection, alg:none, token expiry, XXE, path traversal, stored XSS, and the correct hash_equals decoy. It misses the hardcoded JWT secret as a formal finding and does not include the cookie Secure and SameSite issue, which are both required. The serious D1 problem is the SSRF finding: the AWS metadata endpoint and 0xa9fea9fe bypass are not in the Stage 2 evidence pack, so that evidence is fabricated and I applied the flat fabrication penalty. It does give a correct hash_equals decoy, a few valid findings, and basic detection ideas, but it lacks the required customers-and-naira headline, the real remediation order, and full evidence coverage. D4 is much stronger than the technical middle: it refuses the journalist, limits written content to verified evidence, handles colleague accountability formally, and invokes NDPA notification for the 312 customers. It should cite NDPA sections 40 and 41 by number, but the ethical stance is clear and professional. I did not round this up because fabricated SSRF evidence and the resulting wrong attack chain materially change the submission. The single most important fix is to remove the SSRF/AWS metadata material and rebuild D2 and D3 around the actual SQLi, JWT, XSS, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, and exfiltration evidence.

name: Annet Felly Atemba
feedback: D1 has a useful method section and correctly identifies SQL injection, alg:none, the hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, XXE, path traversal, and open redirect. It misses MD5 password hashing and the cookie flags as proper catalogue rows, and it treats the stored XSS cookie-theft attempt as the decoy rather than listing stored XSS as a real finding. The required decoy is the HS256 hash_equals branch and the b64url helpers, so the D1 decoy row receives no credit. D2 has a reasonable narrative with recon, failed login, SQLi, JWT forgery, users.php data access, XSS, open redirect, XXE, and path traversal mentioned, but the formal hop sections are incomplete and the XSS is incorrectly treated as neutralized rather than still a stored-script risk. D2's CVSS table gives vectors but not strong per-finding scoring, and the 63m naira impact is present but should be tied more explicitly to the sample calculation. D3 includes several important findings and gives a chronological chain with recon, failed login, SQLi, users.php, XSS, open redirect, XXE, and file read. It loses credit for repeating the wrong decoy, for saying the XXE was blocked by WAF without support in the answer key, and for having only one incomplete detection stopgap. D4 covers the journalist, writing, colleague evidence, and NDPC notification, but it says it would confirm the breach informally and does not cite the NDPA sections or affected-subject duty. I looked for a defensible reason to push this higher, but the wrong decoy and incomplete D3 stopgaps keep it in this band. The single most important fix is to make stored XSS a real finding and use hash_equals as the decoy.

name: Olaniyan Mattew Olayinka
feedback: D1 has a solid method section and correctly identifies SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, token lifecycle weakness, open redirect, XXE, data exposure, path traversal, and the hash_equals decoy. It misses the hardcoded JWT secret and cookie flags, and stored XSS is not included as a finding. The D1 appendix gestures at evidence, but several rows do not quote the specific line or timestamp directly in the table. D2 is much thinner than D1: it uses only four main hops, omits recon, failed login, stored XSS, open redirect, and the full capture chronology, and brings in unsupported Task 9 behavioural evidence about 192.168.44.101 and .env retrieval. I treated that as unsupported carryover rather than applying a fabrication penalty because the main chain still rests on valid Stage 2 material. D2's CVSS table covers only a subset of findings, and the business impact gives three sample balances instead of the full sample average and estimated naira exposure. D3 is stronger, with a clear executive summary, useful threat model, correct hash_equals decoy, remediation order, and two practical detection stopgaps. It still carries the unsupported Task 9 .env claim and does not end the summary on the 312-customer and naira headline. D4 refuses the journalist and preserves colleague evidence through formal channels, but it says it would not put technical details in writing when the expected answer is to write verified facts for the official process. It also needs NDPA section 40 and 41 citations and the 72-hour NDPC duty. The single most important fix is to keep the report inside the Stage 2 evidence pack and rebuild D2 around the required chronological hops.

name: Shabnam Qureshi
feedback: D1 is broad and evidence-rich, with SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, client-controlled token validity, cookie flags, open redirect, username enumeration, stored XSS, XXE, and path traversal all represented. The main D1 gap is the decoy: b64url helpers are correctly treated as encoding, but the answer key also expected the HS256 hash_equals branch to be proved safe. D2 has one of the cleaner chronological chains in this chunk, covering recon, failed login, SQLi, dashboard access, users.php enumeration, stored XSS, open redirect, file read, and customer exposure. It loses a bit because the XML XXE path is not fully built as its own hop, and some PoC text still contains leftover template language. D2's CVSS vectors are mostly complete, but the business impact is too cautious in one place, saying the financial magnitude cannot be ascertained even though the sample supports the approximate ₦63m calculation. D3 is strong: it has a clear executive summary, threat model, ten substantiated findings, exploit-chain narrative, remediation order, and two deployable detection stopgaps with false-positive estimates. It also handles the XXE uncertainty honestly rather than overclaiming. D4 is clear and ethical, refuses the journalist, commits to factual documentation, preserves colleague evidence, and names ISC2 Canons I and II. It should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number, and it should make the 72-hour NDPC timeline more explicit. The single most important fix is to add the hash_equals decoy proof and use the sample average to support the naira impact consistently.

name: Victor David Sarkibaka
flagReason: Fabricated or unsupported claims about database backup exfiltration, analyst account compromise, AWS metadata/IAM context, and per-record breach costs.
feedback: D1 covers several real findings, including SQL injection, alg:none, no expiry, hardcoded secret, MD5, and open redirect. It does not catalogue stored XSS, XXE, path traversal, cookie flags, or the real answer-key decoy correctly, and it treats an SSRF theory as the decoy even though the issue shown by the evidence is path traversal and XXE file read. D2 is heavily affected by unsupported claims: database backup exfiltration, analyst sessions leaking, per-record breach costs, and the exact regulatory fine figures are not in the Stage 2 evidence pack. Because those invented details materially change the exploit chain and impact, I applied the flat fabrication penalty. D2 also uses only four hops and skips required recon, failed login, users.php chronology, open redirect, XXE as a separate artefact, and the correct naira exposure calculation. D3 repeats the unsupported AWS IAM and five-analyst-account claims and builds remediation around decommissioning and egress blocking rather than the answer-key remediation logic. It does include some valid findings, but the report does not adequately cover the full evidence set, the real decoy, or detection patterns with reliable false-positive reasoning. D4 focuses on public disclosure strategy rather than the four required ethics prompts, so it does not directly answer the personal journalist request, the internal writing standard, or the colleague-evidence pressure. It does mention ISC2 Canons I and III and NDPA section 40, but it overstates NDPA fine numbers and does not cite the affected-subject duty as section 41. I did not round this up because the unsupported evidence and impact figures are central to the submission. The single most important fix is to remove invented AWS, backup, analyst-compromise, and cost claims and rebuild the report strictly from the five Stage 2 artefacts.

name: Muhammad Alameen Abdullahi
feedback: D1 is a strong catalogue overall: it identifies SQL injection, unsalted MD5, alg:none, hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, role trust, open redirect, stored XSS, path traversal, XXE, and customer-data exposure. The main D1 omission is the cookie Secure and SameSite issue, and the decoy proof focuses on hash_equals without also clearing the Base64URL helpers. D2 reconstructs the major exploitation sequence from SQL injection through users.php, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, and customer-data exposure. It loses credit because it skips the early recon and failed login entries, does not place the events in the full expected timeline, and does not quantify the naira exposure from the exfil sample. The CVSS table has vectors and useful impact language, but several rows are loosely scored and the business impact stops at listing exposed fields. D3 gives Bayo a readable summary, threat model, several substantiated findings, and a practical remediation order. It is missing the required customers-and-naira headline, the disproved decoy section, cookie findings, complete evidence coverage, and false-positive estimates for the two detection stopgaps. D4 refuses the journalist, keeps evidence within official channels, preserves colleague-related evidence, and recognizes NDPA duties. It should cite ISC2 Canon I as well as Canon II, name NDPA sections 40 and 41, and state the 72-hour NDPC notification clock. I looked for a defensible round-up, but the missing naira impact and incomplete D3 decoy and detection work keep it at this score. The single most important fix is to add the cookie finding, the sample-based naira estimate, and the full decoy proof into the report narrative.

name: ALIU MUHAMMED OHIADA
flagReason: D4 appears to answer an unrelated SSRF/IAM ethics scenario rather than the Stage 2 journalist, writing, colleague-evidence, and notification prompt.
feedback: D1 has broad coverage and identifies SQL injection, alg:none, XXE, stored XSS, MD5, hardcoded JWT secret, missing expiry, open redirect, cookie Secure weakness, and path traversal. It misses SameSite and gives only the Base64URL helper as the decoy, so it does not fully prove the HS256 hash_equals branch is safe. D2 contains useful evidence for SQL injection, JWT alg:none, XXE, stored XSS, CVSS vectors, and a customer-and-naira impact estimate. It is substantially weaker as an exploit chain because it omits recon, failed login, users.php as its own data-access hop, open redirect in the hop narrative, and the full file-read chronology, while one XXE section accidentally quotes SQL and JWT code instead of the XML payload. D3 is more complete than D2, with ten findings, risk-based remediation, a decoy discussion, and two deployable detection stopgaps with false-positive estimates. It still misses the SameSite issue, gives only a partial decoy proof, and overstates some evidence, including an asserted XXE response timestamp and a complete customer export path that are not cleanly shown in the supplied artefacts. D4 is the major problem: it answers a different SSRF, IAM credential, and 84,210-record scenario rather than the required Stage 2 ethics prompt about a journalist, what to write, colleague evidence, and breach notification. Because the expected questions are mostly unanswered, it receives only minimal credit for the general refusal to exceed scope and for naming ISC2 Canon II. I did not apply the fabrication penalty because the unsupported SSRF scenario is isolated to the off-prompt ethics answer rather than the technical scoring rows, but it needs senior review. The single most important fix is to replace D4 entirely with an answer anchored to the actual 312-customer Sankofa incident and the NDPA section 40 and 41 duties.

name: Fasola Sunkade
feedback: D1 is careful and evidence-based, covering SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, role trust, missing Secure, missing SameSite, open redirect, stored XSS, and XXE. It does not include path traversal as a separate finding, and the decoy section clears the Base64URL helpers but does not fully discuss the safe HS256 hash_equals branch. D2 is one of the stronger exploit chains in this chunk: it tracks SQLi, JWT forgery, users.php access, XXE, path traversal, stored XSS, open redirect, CVSS vectors, and a sample-based approximately NGN 62.3 million exposure. It loses credit for omitting the recon and failed login entries, for slightly overstating some service relationships, and for saying the real account numbers are in an offline locker in a way that is not necessary to the evidence pack. D3 is a good executive report with a clear customers-and-naira headline, a threat model, prioritized findings, a remediation order based on risk reduction per hour, and two practical detection stopgaps. Its main report gap is the same missing path traversal finding, plus the incomplete decoy proof and a somewhat compressed exploit-chain section. D4 gives a grounded ethics response: it refuses the journalist, limits written content to verified facts, preserves colleague evidence, and commits to breach notification for the 312 affected customers. It correctly invokes ISC2 Canons I and II and NDPA obligations, but it does not cite NDPA section 40, section 41, or the 72-hour NDPC timeline by number. I did round within the stronger band because the work is coherent, tied to evidence, and mostly aligned with the answer key despite the path traversal and decoy gaps. The single most important fix is to add path traversal throughout D1 and D3 and explicitly clear both Base64URL helpers and hash_equals as the decoy.

name: Adeosun john
flagReason: Unsupported business-impact figure of NGN 234,000,000 based on an invented NGN 750,000 per-record liability model, plus unsupported claims about transaction ledgers, encryption schemas, and master ledger extraction.
feedback: D1 correctly identifies alg:none, SQL injection, unsalted MD5, hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, and XXE. It also gives a good decoy discussion for the HS256 hash_equals branch, which is one of the stronger parts of the submission. However, D1 omits stored XSS, path traversal, open redirect, cookie Secure and SameSite flags, and customer-data exposure as catalogue findings, so it covers only about half of the required technical surface. D2 has some valid chain elements, including SQL injection, users.php enumeration, JWT forgery, path traversal or XXE, and customer data exposure. It misses recon, the failed login, stored XSS, open redirect, the expected chronological detail, and most of the required CVSS rows. The largest D2 issue is fabrication: the NGN 750,000 per-record liability model and NGN 234,000,000 total are not derived from the exfil sample, and claims about encryption schemas, transaction ledgers, and master customer ledger extraction are unsupported by the artefacts. D3 repeats that unsupported NGN 234,000,000 impact and overstates the attacker as APT-level with total control over the core ledger, which the evidence does not show. It has an executive summary, threat model, decoy proof, remediation order, and two useful detection stopgaps, but the findings list is incomplete and the chain is materially distorted. D4 is much better than the technical middle: it refuses the journalist, restricts writing to verified logs, preserves colleague evidence, and commits to regulatory escalation despite management pressure. It still needs ISC2 Canon I, NDPA section 40 and section 41 citations, and a precise 72-hour NDPC notification statement. I did not round this up because the unsupported liability calculation is central to the reported impact. The single most important fix is to remove the invented cost model and ledger claims, then rebuild D2 and D3 from the actual 312-row sample and the full set of attack events.

name: David Taiwo A.
feedback: D1 is very strong and covers the expected surface: SQL injection, MD5, stored XSS, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, cookie flags, open redirect, customer-data exposure, path traversal, and XXE. It also gives a well-reasoned decoy verdict for the safe HS256 hash_equals comparison. The only D1 precision gap is that the Base64URL helpers are not separately cleared as part of the decoy, and one reflected-XSS row is extra rather than part of the core answer key. D2 reconstructs the attack well from recon through SQLi, users.php access, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, and exfiltration. It includes CVSS vectors and a sound sample-based estimate of about NGN 63 million, but it does not explicitly include the failed login at 02:14:55 as a hop and occasionally overstates the users.php rows as the same content as the export. D3 is a polished report with a strong customers-and-naira executive headline, threat model, broad findings table, decoy discussion, risk-based remediation order, and two deployable detection stopgaps with false-positive reasoning. It loses only small amounts for the same partial decoy coverage and a minor unsupported reference to an internal API service. D4 handles the journalist, writing boundaries, colleague evidence, and breach-notification obligation clearly. It cites ISC2 Canons I and II and correctly identifies notification to the NDPC and affected customers, but it should name NDPA section 40 and section 41 explicitly and state the 72-hour clock rather than only saying statutory window. I rounded within the top band because the work is comprehensive, evidence-tied, and business-aware. The single most important refinement is to add the failed-login hop and the full Base64URL plus hash_equals decoy proof.

name: Ezekiel Ojo Adedayo
flagReason: Submission is largely from an unrelated scenario and fabricates or imports Elasticsearch, Redis, .env, backup.sql, SSRF/IAM metadata, XML validator, and 84,210-record claims not present in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 is mostly not a Stage 2 findings catalogue. It spends most of its effort on Task 1 style Redis, Elasticsearch, scan-vuln, .env, backup.sql, and 192.168.44.101 material rather than cataloguing the Sankofa legacy-admin vulnerabilities. It does mention several real Stage 2 timestamps, including recon, failed login, SQL injection, users.php, stored XSS, open redirect, and path traversal, but it does not score as a proper finding table and it has no correct decoy analysis. D2 contains a little valid material around SQL injection and stored XSS, but the main chain is built around reflected XSS in search.php, SSRF via XXE, cloud metadata, IAM key theft, and 84,210 records. Those claims are not in the evidence pack and materially replace the required chain, so I applied the fabrication penalty. D2 also misses the actual 312-customer exfil calculation, the real path traversal and XXE evidence, and most of the required CVSS rows. D3 is almost entirely an unrelated SSRF/IAM technical brief with a fake flag, a cloud metadata payload, and 84,210-record board impact. It does not provide Bayo with the requested Sankofa pentest report, answer-key findings, real remediation order, or detection stopgaps for the actual attack. D4 at least answers the ethics structure in a recognizable way: it refuses the journalist, limits unofficial writing, preserves timeline evidence, and says it would report a breach. However, it again uses the wrong 84,210-record scenario, lacks NDPA section 40 and section 41 citations, and does not anchor the notification duty to the actual 312 affected customers. I did not round this up because the unrelated scenario dominates the submission. The single most important fix is to discard the Redis, .env, SSRF/IAM, and 84,210-record material and rebuild all four deliverables from the five Stage 2 artefacts.

name: Godson Enruchi Chukwu
feedback: D1 is solid and evidence-based, with SQL injection, unsalted MD5, hardcoded JWT secret, alg:none, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, and missing Secure cookie flag all present. It also gives the correct hash_equals decoy verdict. The main D1 gaps are the missing SameSite cookie issue, missing token expiry as a stronger catalogue row only partly covered in narrative, and a user-enumeration row that is extra rather than central to the answer key. D2 gives a clear chronological story from SQL injection to users.php, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, and customer-data exposure. It loses credit because recon and the failed login are only summarized, JWT abuse is not built as a chain hop, XXE is not included as a hop, the CVSS table covers only five findings, and the business impact does not calculate the naira exposure. D3 is readable and appropriate for Bayo, with a good executive summary, threat model, decoy discussion, remediation order, and detection stopgaps. It is narrower than expected because several answer-key findings are combined or omitted, including MD5, hardcoded secret, token expiry, cookie flags, and the full naira headline. D4 is strong: it refuses the journalist, writes only evidence-backed facts, preserves colleague-related evidence, and commits to formal breach reporting. It invokes ISC2 Canons I and II and the NDPA notification duty, but it should cite sections 40 and 41 and explicitly say 72 hours. I gave a modest humane lift within this band because the submission is honest, on task, and coherent even where it is incomplete. The single most important fix is to expand D2 and D3 to include JWT, XXE, cookie, and naira-impact details instead of treating SQL injection as the whole story.

name: Iwuji Chikaodi Edith
feedback: D1 is strong and very readable, with SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, open redirect, missing Secure, username enumeration, stored XSS, path traversal, and XXE all tied to evidence. The main D1 gap is that SameSite is not captured, and the decoy clears the Base64URL helpers but does not also discuss the safe HS256 hash_equals comparison. D2 is excellent on chronology and includes the failed login, SQL injection, users.php, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, customer-data exfiltration, CVSS rows, and business impact. It loses a little for not including the initial 02:14:08 recon hop and for using a midpoint NGN 46.8 million estimate rather than the stronger sample-average calculation. It loses some credit for the partial decoy proof, the missing SameSite flag, and a small unsupported claim that the panel shares auth tokens with an internal API service. The single most important refinement is to add SameSite and hash_equals coverage, then use the sample-average naira calculation for a tighter impact estimate.

name: Iengem Jemima Gbamwuan
flagReason: Unsupported SSRF/cloud metadata/IAM material appears in D1, D3, and D4 and replaces the real XXE/path-traversal evidence in parts of the submission.
feedback: D1 shows effort and includes several real findings, including SQL injection, alg:none, stored XSS, path traversal, and open redirect. It misses or weakly covers unsalted MD5, the hardcoded JWT secret, cookie flags, XXE as the actual XML issue, and the correct decoy. The decoy verdict is also wrong because users.php data exposure is not the answer-key decoy; the expected false positive is the Base64URL helper and the safe HS256 hash_equals comparison. D1 also introduces unsupported SSRF and cloud metadata evidence, including 169.254.169.254 and IAM-role material, which is not in the Stage 2 evidence pack. D2 gives a basic chain from SQL injection to dashboard access, users.php, stored XSS, open redirect, and path traversal, but it omits recon, failed login, JWT abuse as a real hop, XXE, the final customer export, and a proper naira impact estimate. Its CVSS table mostly uses placeholder vectors, so the scoring evidence is thin. D3 has a readable executive summary and some useful remediation and detection content, but it again builds around SSRF and cloud exposure instead of the actual XXE file-read issue. The D3 report also lacks a proper decoy discussion, complete findings, the sample-based naira headline, and the expected detection stopgaps for the real chain. D4 gives a reasonable ethics stance on the journalist, breach notification, colleague evidence, and ISC2 Canons I and II, and it mentions a 72-hour NDPA duty. It loses credit for saying the technical breach details should not be put in writing and for citing section 40 only without section 41. I did not round this up because the unsupported SSRF material is repeated across the submission. The single most important fix is to remove the cloud metadata path and rebuild the XML finding as XXE to file:///etc/passwd, with the correct decoy and naira impact.

name: Rotimi Omobolanle
feedback: D1 is the strongest part of this submission and covers SQL injection, unsalted MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, role trust, missing Secure and SameSite, open redirect, XXE, and path traversal. It also includes reflected XSS, which is extra, but it does not list the stored XSS capture as the main XSS finding. The decoy correctly clears the Base64URL helpers, but it does not also explain why the HS256 hash_equals branch is safe. D2 reconstructs a sensible chain through SQL injection, users.php, XSS testing, open redirect, file read, and XXE, and it includes CVSS vectors plus a reasonable statement that the sample implies tens of millions of naira in exposure. It loses credit because the recon and failed-login events are missing, JWT abuse is not a hop, stored XSS is underdeveloped, and the naira calculation is not fully worked from the sample. It has a short executive summary, remediation order, and two detection stopgaps, but it lacks a threat model, findings table, decoy discussion, exploit-chain narrative, detailed business impact, and false-positive reasoning beyond brief labels. D4 is professional and covers the journalist, writing boundaries, colleague evidence, ISC2 Canons I and II, and the need for regulatory reporting. It loses credit because the one independent action is evidence preservation rather than ensuring notification, and it does not cite NDPA sections 40 and 41 or the 72-hour NDPC clock. I did not round this higher because D3 is a major deliverable and is too abbreviated. The single most important fix is to expand D3 into a full report with findings, chain, decoy, customers-and-naira impact, and concrete detection stopgaps.

name: Adeoye Olude
missingPieces: D2 exploit chain & CVSS missing entirely (0). D1 only captured 2 of 10 key findings (JWT alg:none, XXE); missed SQLi, unsalted MD5, hardcoded secret, no token expiry, stored XSS, path traversal, open redirect, cookie Secure/SameSite. D3 business impact inflated and ungrounded (cited 120k-180k customers and billions NGN vs the 312-row evidence). D4 missing NDPA s40/s41 and NDPC 72h citation.
feedback: Adeoye, you submitted three of the four deliverables (D1 findings, D3 report, D4 ethics), and the work you did turn in shows real security instinct, so let me grade it fairly before naming what was missing. On D1 you wrote a clean, disciplined catalogue, but only two of the ten target vulnerabilities are actually present and properly evidenced: JWT alg:none (CWE-347, with the correct {"alg":"none"} header line) and XXE (CWE-611, with the file:///etc/passwd payload). Both of those are full-credit findings, and I gave you a little extra for correctly reasoning that the signature-pattern observation was a non-exploitable false positive rather than chasing it. The trouble is that the other four entries in your catalogue are really sub-aspects of those same two bugs, so the eight remaining key findings (SQL injection in login.php, unsalted MD5, the hardcoded sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 secret, missing token expiry, the stored XSS beacon, path traversal, open redirect, and the missing cookie Secure/SameSite flags) simply are not there, which is why D1 lands at 7 of 30. D3 is your strongest piece: you ordered remediation by effort rather than by CVSS exactly as the brief asks, and you gave two genuine detection stopgaps with a data field and a false-positive rate each, which is precisely what was wanted. I docked D3 mainly because the business impact section is inflated and ungrounded, since you quoted 120,000 to 180,000 customers and billions of naira when the evidence shows 312 affected customers and tens of millions in balances. That is an overreach in framing rather than a faked artifact, so I did not apply a fabrication penalty, but please anchor impact to the actual exfil evidence next time. D4 reads in a confident, honest, first-person voice, you answered all four prompts, and you cited ISC2 canons by number, so that earned solid credit; it fell short of full marks only because the NDPA 2023 obligations stayed generic, with no section 40 (NDPC 72-hour notification) or section 41 (data-subject) citations. Now the part I have to state plainly and kindly: the D2 exploit chain and CVSS deliverable was not in your folder at all, so that entire 35-point section scored zero, and that single absence is the largest reason your total sits where it does. The most important next step is to build and submit that D2 exploit chain, walking the attacker timeline from recon at 02:14:08 through the SQLi at 02:15:31 to the 312-row exfil, with a scored CVSS vector and justification, because you clearly have the analytical skill to do it well.

name: Nnanna Adaobi Evelyn
feedback: D1 is very strong and covers nearly the full technical surface, including SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, missing Secure and SameSite, open redirect, stored and reflected XSS, path traversal, and XXE. It also gives the correct safe hash_equals decoy verdict, though it does not separately clear the Base64URL helper functions. D2 has strong evidence for SQL injection, JWT alg:none, path traversal, XXE, CVSS vectors, and a sample-based impact estimate around NGN 62.9 million. It loses more than D1 because the exploit chain skips recon, failed login, users.php, stored XSS, and open redirect, and it overstates the route as an extraction of the production ledger through XXE. It is too narrow, though: only four findings are substantiated, so MD5, hardcoded secret, token expiry, cookies, XSS, and open redirect are not properly carried into the final report. D3 also repeats the unsupported claim that the legacy app shares authentication components with /api/v1/internal. D4 is strong and grounded: it refuses the journalist, limits writing to verified evidence, sends the full evidence chain to Amaka and Legal, and states the 72-hour notification duty to the NDPC and affected data subjects. It should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number and bring in ISC2 Canon I as well as Canon II. I did not round this into the 80s because D2 and D3 narrow the attack chain too much despite the excellent D1. The single most important fix is to carry all D1 findings into D2 and D3 instead of focusing mainly on SQLi, JWT, path traversal, and XXE.

name: Ojukwu Immaculeta chiamaka
feedback: D1 is mostly on the right evidence pack and identifies SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, missing expiry, hardcoded secret, insecure cookies, missing SameSite, open redirect, stored XSS, and path traversal. name: Folayan Olumide
feedback: D1 has several strong rows, including SQL injection, alg:none, XXE, path traversal, MD5, hardcoded secret, stored XSS, and missing expiry. It misses cookie Secure and SameSite, open redirect as a catalogue row, and customer-data exposure, and its decoy is wrong. The safe construct was not alg:none; alg:none is a real finding, while the expected decoy was the Base64URL helper and HS256 hash_equals comparison. D2 is more coherent than D1's decoy section, with a chain through failed login context, SQL injection, JWT, file read, XXE, exfiltration, CVSS rows, and a good sample-based estimate of about NGN 63 million. It still misses users.php as its own hop, stored XSS and open redirect as active chain events, recon at 02:14:08, and a complete CVSS table for all answer-key findings. D3 has a useful executive summary, threat model, chain timeline, remediation order, and two detection stopgaps. It loses credit because it repeats the wrong decoy, says XXE was blocked by WAF while treating path traversal as the successful file read, and omits cookie flags, MD5, and missing expiry from the final findings table. D4 is strong and practical: it refuses the journalist, limits writing to corroborated facts, preserves evidence about the senior colleague, and commits to reporting data exfiltration through compliance. It cites ISC2 Canons I, II, and III and invokes NDPA notification duties, but it should cite sections 40 and 41 and the 72-hour clock explicitly. I did not round this higher because the D1 decoy error and missing cookie findings are material. The single most important fix is to replace the alg:none decoy with the Base64URL and hash_equals decoy, then carry cookie and open-redirect findings into D1 through D3.

name: Olayinka Samuel Ojo
flagReason: Unsupported cross-stage claims about IAM token extraction, Elasticsearch holding 84,210 records, scan-full infrastructure, trust-score movement, and broader cloud infrastructure compromise.
feedback: D1 is excellent overall, covering SQL injection and MD5, alg:none, missing exp and nbf, hardcoded secret, role trust, open redirect, stored XSS, XXE, path traversal, cookie flags, and username reflection. The main D1 gap is the partial decoy: it correctly clears the Base64URL helpers but does not also clear the safe HS256 hash_equals comparison. D2 is strong on the actual Sankofa chain, including SQL injection, users.php access, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, CVSS, and a well-supported NGN 63 million impact estimate. It loses credit for omitting the failed-login hop and for importing unsupported claims about /api/v1/internal, IAM token extraction, Elasticsearch, 84,210 customer documents, and a trust-score drop. Those unsupported claims materially inflate scope, so I applied the fabrication penalty. D3 is otherwise polished, with a strong executive summary, threat model, findings summary, decoy, exploit chain, remediation order, detection stopgaps, and evidence appendix. It is marked down for the same unsupported cross-stage cloud and 84,210-record material, plus unsupported statements such as admin cookies harvested for six hours and the app being Django rather than the PHP evidence pack. D4 is one of the stronger ethics responses in this chunk: it refuses the journalist cleanly, keeps writing in official channels, preserves colleague timeline evidence, and raises the NDPA section 40 72-hour notification duty. It should cite section 41 for affected data subjects and include ISC2 Canon II alongside Canon I. I did not round this further because the unsupported cloud/IAM material is repeated in D2 and D3. The single most important fix is to remove all Elasticsearch, IAM, 84,210-record, and trust-score claims and keep the report strictly on the 312-customer Stage 2 evidence.

name: Liliyosa Mbakureya
flagReason: Unsupported claims about shared authentication, internal service exposure, extra PII fields, and a PDF/SSRF decoy not present in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 identifies most of the real technical weaknesses, including SQL injection, MD5 hashing, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing token expiry, stored XSS, XXE, path traversal, open redirect, and cookie weaknesses. The main D1 loss is the decoy: the safe construct was the Base64URL helper and especially the HS256 hash_equals branch, while the PDF/SSRF framing is not supported by this evidence pack. D2 gives a usable chain through SQL injection, admin access, data exposure, and file-read style weaknesses, but it is too compressed and misses several required capture-backed hops, including recon at 02:14:08, the failed login at 02:14:55, stored XSS at 02:18:47, and open redirect at 02:21:13. Its CVSS and impact discussion are present but not consistently complete, and the business impact does not land clearly on 312 customers plus a naira estimate from the sample. D3 has the shape of a board-facing report, with an executive summary, threat model, findings, remediation, and detection ideas. It loses substantial credit because it imports unsupported shared-authentication and internal-service claims, adds extra data fields not shown in the sample, and does not keep the report tightly anchored to the Stage 2 artifacts. D4 states a general ethical preference for truthfulness and escalation, but it does not directly answer the journalist prompt, what should be put in writing, the colleague evidence problem, and the one action to take regardless of the manager. It also misses the load-bearing NDPA section 40 and section 41 analysis tied to the 312 affected customers. I did not round this higher because the unsupported scope expansion repeats across deliverables and triggers the fabrication penalty. The single most important fix is to remove unsupported SSRF, shared-authentication, and extra-field claims, then rebuild D2 and D3 around the exact capture timestamps and the 312-row exfil sample.

name: Philip Oyeyemi Adeyanju
feedback: D1 is solid on several important findings, including SQL injection, MD5 hashing, JWT alg:none, missing expiry, role trust, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, and the safe hash_equals decoy. It loses credit because path traversal and missing Secure and SameSite cookie attributes are not handled as full findings, the hardcoded secret is not carried as a clear catalogue item, and the decoy proof does not also mention the Base64URL helpers. D2 reconstructs a meaningful attack path through SQL injection, dashboard access, user exposure, XSS, open redirect, XXE, and JWT abuse, with CVSS work that is more complete than average. It still misses the opening recon and failed-login timestamps, and the business impact never becomes the required customers-and-naira headline from the 312-row export and redacted balance sample. D3 is a useful client report: it has an executive summary, threat model, evidence-tied findings, a decoy discussion, remediation, and detection controls. The final report is held back by the same omissions as D1 and D2, especially the missing cookie and path traversal treatment, the thin naira impact, and incomplete carry-through of all ten expected findings. D4 makes the right broad ethical call by refusing the journalist and preserving verified evidence for internal and legal channels. It names professional duties, but it does not cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 with the 72-hour NDPC duty and affected-subject notification, and the independent action is less concrete than it should be. I looked for a defensible way to move this into the high 70s, but the missing path, cookie, and naira details are too central. The single most important fix is to make the 312-customer, sample-based naira exposure the spine of D2 and D3, while adding the two missing access-control findings.

name: Aselemi Kitoye
feedback: D1 is short but on the right case, with SQL injection, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, and XXE present. It misses unsalted MD5 and missing Secure and SameSite cookie attributes, and the decoy proof only covers Base64URL encoding rather than also explaining why hash_equals makes the HS256 comparison safe. D2 is the strongest part of the submission because it follows a recognizable chain from recon through SQL injection, user exposure, XSS, redirect, file read, and XXE. It still loses credit for omitting the failed-login hop, not using JWT as a meaningful chain element, and keeping several CVSS rows too thin, but the NGN 63 million sample-based impact is a good piece of work. D3 has the required sections in miniature, including an executive note, threat model, findings, decoy, remediation, and detection stopgaps. The problem is depth: the report is too compressed to persuade Bayo, findings are not consistently tied to exact evidence, the remediation order is not argued enough by effort-to-risk, and the detections need exact fields or patterns plus false-positive expectations. D4 has the right ethical instinct, refusing public speculation and escalating through proper channels. It does not cite ISC2 canons by number in a load-bearing way, and it misses NDPA section 40, section 41, the 72-hour NDPC clock, and the specific affected-customer notification duty. I did not round this higher because D3 is too thin even though D2 has a good impact estimate. The single most important fix is to expand the final report into evidence-backed findings with exact timestamps, CVSS vectors, and concrete detection rules rather than brief summaries.

name: Quadri Durodola
flagReason: Unsupported claims that the attacker obtained temporary cloud/IAM credentials and breached cloud-metadata trust, which are not present in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 is careful and well-evidenced for SQL injection, MD5 hashing, open redirect, reflected and stored XSS class evidence, mass user disclosure, alg:none, missing token expiry, XXE, and path traversal. It loses material credit because the hardcoded secret and missing Secure and SameSite cookie attributes are absent, and the decoy is wrong: Token 1 is not the expected safe construct, while the Base64URL helpers and HS256 hash_equals branch needed to be cleared. D2 is excellent on the actual chronology, with recon, failed login, SQL injection, users.php disclosure, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, full CVSS work, and a strong NGN 63 million impact estimate from the sample. The D2 mark is held just below full because it repeats some unsupported cloud-metadata framing and does not keep every architectural conclusion inside the artifacts. D3 is polished and highly readable, with a strong executive summary, threat model, findings table, exploit chain, remediation order by risk reduction per hour, and two concrete detection stopgaps. However, the executive summary and threat model make unsupported claims that the attacker obtained temporary cloud IAM credentials and breached Sankofa's cloud account, which is not in the Stage 2 evidence and materially inflates the incident, so I applied the fabrication penalty. D4 has a mature voice, refuses press speculation, anchors the decision in the 312 affected customers, and cites ISC2 Canon I, Canon II, and NDPA section 40 with the 72-hour notification duty. It misses the colleague-evidence prompt, does not clearly state what will be put in writing, and should cite section 41 separately for affected data subjects. I did not round this higher because the cloud/IAM claim is prominent in the client-facing report. The single most important fix is to remove all cloud credential and IAM-role language, then replace the decoy with the Base64URL and hash_equals analysis.

name: Moshood Bushroh
feedback: D1 is a strong catalogue with a clear method and evidence for hardcoded secret, alg:none, XXE, SQL injection, MD5, missing exp, open redirect, reflected XSS, stored XSS, and path traversal. It loses credit for omitting the missing Secure and SameSite cookie finding and for using the wrong decoy, because the count(parts) guard was not the expected safe construct and the answer needed the Base64URL helper plus HS256 hash_equals comparison. D2 reconstructs most of the attack well, including recon, SQL injection, dashboard access, users.php, stored XSS, XXE, path traversal, exfiltration, CVSS vectors, and a BoltCash impact paragraph. It misses the failed credential attempt at 02:14:55, does not include open redirect or JWT as meaningful chain events, and some CVSS labels and scores do not match their own vectors. D3 is readable and useful for Bayo, with a customer-and-naira executive headline, threat model, findings, chain, remediation by effort-to-risk, and two practical detection stopgaps. The D3 deductions come from the wrong decoy, the missing cookie issue, several shaky CVSS severities, and an over-narrow view of the earliest break as SQL injection without also addressing the independent alg:none path. D4 refuses the journalist, documents evidence, preserves colleague-related facts, and names the 312-customer exposure as the reason to notify regulators and affected users. It cites ISC2 Canon I and Canon II, but it does not cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number and it says notification happens after 72 hours rather than within 72 hours. I looked for a defensible push into the 80s, but the wrong decoy and missing cookie finding are too material. The single most important fix is to replace the decoy section with the Base64URL and hash_equals analysis, then add the missing cookie controls across D1 and D3.

name: Alaafiaoluwa Ajayi
flagReason: Unsupported SSRF, cloud metadata, IAM credential extraction, APT, and AWS takeover claims not present in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 gets real credit for identifying alg:none, the hardcoded secret, missing token expiry, missing Secure cookie flag, SQL injection, XXE, and the Base64URL helper decoy. It misses unsalted MD5 as a standalone finding, stored XSS, path traversal, open redirect, and SameSite, and it also invents SSRF with IAM extraction from cloud metadata, which is not in the Stage 2 artifacts. D2 has a chronological structure and includes recon, the failed credential test, JWT alg:none, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, CVSS vectors, and some business discussion. The chain is materially weakened because it makes alg:none the main active route instead of the observed SQL injection at 02:15:31, treats users.php as reached by a forged token, and repeats the unsupported SSRF and cloud-token story. D3 is polished in tone, with an executive summary, threat model, findings, decoy, remediation order, and detection controls. The substance is too narrow and inflated: it omits many answer-key findings, centers unauthenticated cloud metadata and AWS credential compromise, and cites NDPA section 48 instead of the breach-notification duties in sections 40 and 41. D4 is much better than the technical report, because it refuses the journalist, limits writing to verified forensics, preserves colleague evidence, and escalates NDPA notification despite management pressure. It still needs section 40 for NDPC notification, section 41 for affected data subjects, and a more accurate ISC2 Canon IV statement. I did not round this upward because the unsupported cloud and IAM material repeats across D1 to D3 and triggers the fabrication penalty. The single most important fix is to remove every SSRF, AWS, IAM, and cloud-metadata claim, then rebuild the chain around the observed SQL injection, users.php dump, XSS, open redirect, XXE, and path traversal events.

name: Mercy Itunuoluwa Olalere
flagReason: D1 fabricates an SSRF request to 169.254.169.254 and returned AWS IMDS credentials, which are not present in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 has a solid method and correctly identifies SQL injection, missing token expiry, alg:none, XXE, open redirect, and missing Secure cookie flag, with a correct Base64URL helper decoy. It loses credit because the hardcoded secret evidence is only a vague comment rather than the actual sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 value, MD5 is missing as a finding, stored XSS and path traversal are absent, SameSite is not covered, and the SSRF/AWS metadata row is fabricated. D2 is stronger than D1 because it gives a coherent chain through SQL injection, alg:none, XXE, and bulk customer export, with PoCs, CVSS vectors, and a sample-based naira estimate. It still misses recon at 02:14:08, the failed login, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal as its own observed hop, and several answer-key findings in the CVSS table. D3 has a persuasive executive summary, threat model, remediation order by effort, and concrete SQLi and alg:none detection stopgaps. It is marked down for carrying only five main findings, omitting MD5, hardcoded secret, stored XSS, path traversal, and cookie flags from the client report, and for leaning on the shared internal-service scope without enough direct evidence in the report body. D4 is strong, human, and complete on the four prompts: it refuses the journalist, controls what goes in writing, preserves colleague evidence, and insists on breach notification. It cites ISC2 Canon III and Canon II in a load-bearing way and anchors the action to the 312 customer records, but it should cite NDPA sections 40 and 41 by number. I did not round this higher because the D1 fabricated SSRF row and the missing core findings outweigh the good structure. The single most important fix is to delete the AWS metadata claim and add the missing MD5, stored XSS, path traversal, and cookie findings across all three technical deliverables.

name: Jessica ighoraye
flagReason: Unsupported NGN 46.8 million impact estimate based on a per-record benchmark rather than the exfil sample balance data.
feedback: D1 is a decent evidence catalogue with alg:none, hardcoded secret, SQL injection, unsalted MD5, observed SQLi exploitation, open redirect, bulk user exposure, missing exp and nbf, XXE, and customer export scope. It misses stored XSS, path traversal as a catalogue finding, and missing Secure and SameSite cookie attributes, and its decoy is not the expected Base64URL or hash_equals construct. D2 lays out a clear chain through SQL injection, users.php exposure, path traversal, XXE, and customer export, and it is honest that the export request itself is not directly visible in the HTTP capture. It loses credit for omitting recon, the failed login, stored XSS, open redirect, and a properly sample-derived naira impact, and the NGN 46.8 million figure is based on an unsupported per-record benchmark rather than the provided balance sample. D3 is one of the stronger parts of the submission, with a readable executive summary, threat model, findings matrix, chain, CVSS table, remediation order, and two deployable detection controls. It still repeats the unsupported NGN 46.8 million estimate, uses the wrong decoy, and leaves out MD5, stored XSS, open redirect, and cookie flags from the final findings set. D4 is direct and grounded: it refuses the journalist, states what should not go in writing, preserves colleague evidence, cites ISC2 Canon I and Canon II, and insists on notifying the NDPC and affected data subjects. It should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number and tie the 72-hour deadline explicitly to section 40. I did not round this higher because the unsupported impact calculation triggers the fabrication penalty and the technical reports miss several required findings. The single most important fix is to replace the per-record NGN estimate with the sample-balance calculation and carry stored XSS, path traversal, and cookie flags into D1 through D3.

name: Fatima Nazreen Khan
feedback: D1 is strong and methodical, with clear evidence for SQL injection, unsalted MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, token expiry weakness, open redirect, cookie Secure and SameSite issues, and XXE. It also gives a good Base64URL decoy explanation, but it misses stored XSS and path traversal as catalogue findings and does not explicitly clear the HS256 hash_equals branch. D2 is one of the better exploit-chain submissions, with recon, failed login, SQL injection, users.php, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, exfiltration, and a correct sample-derived estimate of roughly NGN 63 million. Its main D2 weakness is that the CVSS table is more score-based than vector-and-justification based for every finding, and it treats a forged alg:none request as more observed than the evidence clearly proves. D3 is concise but actionable: it has a customer-and-naira executive headline, threat model, findings, decoy, exploit chain, remediation by risk reduction per hour, and concrete SQLi and alg:none detection stopgaps. It loses some credit because stored XSS is not fully elevated into the findings section, the decoy only covers Base64URL, and the report compresses several findings too much for a board packet. D4 makes the correct call on the journalist, keeps writing limited to verified technical work, preserves the senior-colleague timeline, and insists on breach notification for 312 customers. It cites ISC2 Canon I and Canon II, but it should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number and state the 72-hour NDPC deadline explicitly. I gave the humane benefit here because the core chain, impact math, and remediation logic are all defensible. The single most important fix is to add stored XSS and path traversal to D1, then expand the decoy to include hash_equals.

name: Ajao Mariam Blessing
feedback: D1 is much too narrow, because it focuses almost entirely on JWT issues: missing signature, alg:none, missing expiry, client-controlled expiry, and a weak or guessable HS256 secret. It earns decoy credit for explaining that HS256 itself is not inherently unsafe when the secret is strong and verification is enforced, but it misses SQL injection, MD5, the actual hardcoded sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 secret, stored XSS, XXE, path traversal, open redirect, and cookie flags as catalogue findings. D2 is considerably stronger than D1, with a chain through recon, SQL injection, users.php, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, exfiltration, CVSS rows, and a reasonable impact discussion. It still misses the failed-login hop, does not bring XXE into the chain, leaves alg:none out of the chain despite D1 focusing on it, and the NGN 59M to NGN 187M range should be replaced by the sample-derived calculation around NGN 63M. D3 is readable and has the right sections: executive summary, threat model, findings, decoy, chain, CVSS, remediation, and detections. It loses credit because several findings are still absent or thin, the financial headline says only millions of naira instead of a calculated customer-and-naira number, and the CVSS table uses rough scores rather than complete vectors for every item. D4 is sensible and grounded: it refuses the journalist, says what will and will not go in writing, preserves colleague evidence, cites ISC2 Canon I and II, and escalates breach notification for 312 users. It should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number and include the 72-hour NDPC deadline. I did not round this higher because D1 omits most of the evidence pack's non-JWT attack surface. The single most important fix is to rebuild D1 as a full findings catalogue, then make D2 and D3 use the same complete set of findings.

name: Janet Michael
feedback: D1 is detailed and well anchored, with SQL injection, MD5, hardcoded secret, alg:none, missing token expiry, role trust, insecure cookies, open redirect, XXE, and a correct hash_equals decoy explanation. It loses credit because stored XSS is missing and path traversal is not separated as its own catalogue finding even though the file-read evidence appears elsewhere. D2 gives a broad technical reconstruction with recon, failed login, SQL injection, dashboard and users.php access, JWT weaknesses, XXE, file access, data exposure, and a clear statement that 312 customer records were affected. It does not fully develop stored XSS and open redirect as active hops, and it avoids the expected naira exposure calculation from the 20-row sample, so the impact row is incomplete. D3 is clear and useful, with an executive summary, threat model, evidence-tied findings, the correct hash_equals decoy, chain narrative, remediation priorities, and SQLi plus alg:none detection stopgaps. It is marked down because it omits stored XSS, does not give a proper customers-and-naira headline, and describes the business impact as data exposure without doing the sample balance estimate. D4 has the right general instinct: do not leak to the journalist, protect customers, avoid blame games, and escalate the incident through proper security channels. It is too thin for the rubric because it does not clearly answer what will and will not be put in writing, does not preserve colleague evidence in a concrete way, and does not cite NDPA sections 40 and 41 or the 72-hour notification duty. I did not round this into the 80s because D2 and D3 leave out the naira impact and D4 is underdeveloped. The single most important fix is to add the sample-derived NGN exposure and a fuller ethics response with NDPA section citations.

name: Muhammad Abdullah Azib
feedback: D1 is a very strong catalogue of the actual legacy-admin flaws, with all ten core findings present and tied to source lines, token artefacts, or capture timestamps, including the hardcoded secret, no expiry, stored XSS, XXE, path traversal, open redirect, and the missing Secure and SameSite cookie controls. The main D1 weakness is the decoy analysis: it argues that MD5 is not a decoy, which is true but not the safe construct the exercise expected, so it misses the Base64URL helper and the safe hash_equals HS256 comparison. D2 is excellent on chronology, with recon, failed login, SQLi, user enumeration, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, and the 312-row exfiltration connected to PoCs and timestamps. The CVSS work is unusually complete and the naira impact is sensibly derived from the sample balances, although the full chain could separate confirmed data theft from possible follow-on credential theft more carefully. D3 reads like a report Bayo could act on, with a clear 312-customer and Naira headline, a practical effort-to-risk remediation order, and useful stopgap detections with false-positive reasoning. D3 loses credit because it repeats the wrong decoy instead of disproving the safe Base64URL and hash_equals code, and it briefly calls the PHP app a Django admin panel. D4 answers the journalist and evidence-retention issues in a mature voice, names ISC2 Canons 1 and 3, and anchors the duty to the 312-row export. It should cite the NDPA duties by the expected sections, section 40 for notifying the NDPC within 72 hours and section 41 for notifying high-risk affected data subjects. The single most important fix is to replace the MD5 decoy discussion with the actual safe Base64URL and hash_equals decoy analysis.

name: Dakang Victor Ladat
flagReason: Unsupported business-impact figures in D2 and D3, including a 10,000,000 Naira fine, 50,000 Naira per customer remediation cost, 45,000,000 Naira opportunity loss, and a 70,600,000 Naira total that do not trace to the exfil sample.
feedback: D1 is careful and evidence-led, covering most of the expected findings with OWASP and CWE mapping, including SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, the hardcoded secret, missing expiry, open redirect, stored XSS, path traversal, and the missing Secure and SameSite cookie controls. It deserves credit for correctly identifying the Base64URL helper as safe, but it only partially handles the decoy because it does not also discuss the safe hash_equals HS256 comparison, and it misses XXE as a finding even though the evidence pack includes the XML artefact. D2 gives a coherent four-hop chain and useful PoCs, but it omits important chronological events such as recon, the failed credential guess, stored XSS, and open redirect, and its grouped CVSS table is much thinner than a full finding-by-finding vector and justification.
