The serious D2 problem is fabricated impact math: the 10,000,000 Naira fine, 50,000 Naira per customer remediation model, 45,000,000 Naira opportunity loss, and 70,600,000 Naira total are not derived from the provided sample, so I applied the fabrication penalty and did not round this mark up. D3 is useful as an executive report, with a clear recommendation to isolate the legacy portal, a reasonable remediation order by effort-to-risk, and two deployable detection ideas. D3 still repeats the same unsupported 70,600,000 Naira impact and overstates some blast-radius language, and it omits or downplays stored XSS and token expiry in the report findings. D4 is one of the stronger ethics responses in this chunk: it answers the journalist, what goes into writing, the colleague evidence problem, and the action to take under management pressure. It cites ISC2 canons meaningfully and names NDPA section 40 with the 72-hour NDPC duty, though it should also explicitly cite section 41 for high-risk affected data subjects. The single most important fix is to keep the impact calculation tied to the 312-row sample and its balance values instead of inventing fines and opportunity-loss figures.

name: KABIRU SOLIU
feedback: D1 identifies several real vulnerabilities and ties them to evidence, including SQL injection, alg:none, unsalted MD5, stored XSS, path traversal, XXE, open redirect, and the missing Secure cookie flag. It misses the hardcoded JWT secret, missing exp and nbf token lifetime controls, and SameSite, and the decoy section disproves brute force rather than the actual safe Base64URL helper and hash_equals comparison. D2 reconstructs a basic compromise path from SQL injection to JWT abuse, user table access, and file read, and it gives CVSS vectors for the findings it chose. The chain is incomplete because it skips recon, the failed login, stored XSS, open redirect, and the exact 312-row exfiltration impact, and it does not translate the sample balances into a defensible Naira exposure. D3 has a readable executive summary, a threat model, a short exploit chain, and a sensible first remediation step to firewall or disable legacy-admin. It remains too thin for the reporting row because it only carries a subset of findings, uses the wrong decoy again, and gives generic detection stopgaps without exact fields, patterns, or false-positive rates. D4 cites ISC2 Canons 1, 2, and 4 and correctly recognises the NDPA section 40 duty to notify the NDPC within 72 hours. It does not directly answer the journalist question, what should be put in writing, how to handle the colleague evidence, or the single action to take if management resists, and it does not cite section 41 for affected high-risk data subjects. I looked for a defensible way to push this higher, but the missing hardcoded secret, expiry issue, correct decoy, exact impact calculation, and prompt-specific ethics answers keep it below the next band. The single most important fix is to work from the answer-key evidence list and explicitly cover all ten findings plus the actual safe decoy.

name: Najma Omary
feedback: D1 has a clear method and good evidence for several major flaws, especially SQL injection, alg:none, XXE, stored XSS, path traversal, user enumeration, and open redirect. It misses three answer-key items as standalone findings: unsalted MD5 password hashing, missing exp and nbf token lifetime controls, and the missing Secure and SameSite cookie attributes. The hardcoded secret appears only inside the decoy discussion, so it earns partial recognition but should have been a full finding with the value sankofa-legacy-admin-2019. D1 also uses the wrong decoy, treating the exploitable JWT implementation as the target rather than disproving the safe Base64URL helper and hash_equals HS256 comparison. D2 is much stronger, with a useful chronological chain from recon and failed login through SQLi, user access, stored XSS, open redirect, JWT weakness, XXE, path traversal, and exfiltration. The D2 CVSS work is present for several findings and the impact is tied to 312 customers and Naira exposure, although the balance estimate is not as well reconciled to the provided sample as it should be. D3 gives Bayo a usable report with a business-facing summary, threat model, chain, remediation order, and two detection stopgaps. D3 loses credit for repeating the wrong decoy, grouping several JWT issues too broadly, and using a medium false-positive claim where the exact fields and alert logic needed sharper treatment. D4 answers the journalist, written-record, colleague-evidence, and notification-pressure parts in a practical way, and it cites ISC2 Canons I and II. It should cite NDPA section 40 with the 72-hour NDPC duty and section 41 for affected high-risk data subjects. The single most important fix is to return to the D1 answer key and add the missing MD5, token expiry, cookie, hardcoded secret, and actual safe-decoy analysis.

name: Ayodeji Ogungbire
feedback: D1 is readable and captures several real findings with evidence, including SQL injection, MD5 password storage, alg:none, missing JWT expiry, stored XSS, open redirect, and path traversal. It misses the hardcoded JWT secret, XXE, and the missing Secure and SameSite cookie controls, and the decoy section disproves password guessing instead of the safe Base64URL and hash_equals construct. D2 explains the basic attack path from SQL injection to user information, stored XSS, open redirect, and arbitrary file read. It leaves out recon, the failed credential guess, JWT token abuse, XXE, and the full 312-row export chain, and its CVSS table gives severity labels rather than complete vectors with justification. D2 also describes affected customer fields but does not calculate any sample-based Naira exposure. D3 has a coherent executive summary and a sensible remediation list, including parameterized queries, JWT replacement, file-read fixes, XSS controls, redirect validation, and MD5 replacement. The report remains generic because it repeats the wrong decoy, omits key findings, gives no Naira headline, and provides detection stopgaps without exact fields, patterns, or false-positive rates. D4 cites ISC2 Canons 1 and 2 and recognises the general NDPA duty to protect personal data. It does not answer the specific journalist, written-evidence, senior-colleague, and manager-pressure scenario directly, and it does not cite section 40, section 41, or the 72-hour NDPC requirement. The single most important fix is to use the provided evidence pack to cover all ten required findings and the real safe decoy before writing the chain and final report.

name: Lucky Ogwuazor
flagReason: D3 uses an unsupported 124,000,000 Naira customer-funds exposure figure that does not trace to the exfil sample or to the D2 calculation.
feedback: D1 is excellent and close to complete, with all ten answer-key findings present, evidence citations, OWASP and CWE mapping, and the correct hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019. It also correctly handles the decoy by explaining why the HS256 branch using hash_equals is not exploitable for timing or key-confusion attacks, while distinguishing that safe block from the real alg:none flaw. D2 reconstructs SQL injection, JWT forgery, XXE, and data exfiltration, and it gives a sample-based Naira estimate of about 64.5 million that is close to the expected exposure range. D2 still omits several important observed chain steps, including recon, the failed credential guess, stored XSS, open redirect, and the path traversal confirmation, and its CVSS table covers only three grouped findings. D3 has a professional executive frame, a threat model, a correct decoy discussion, and actionable stopgaps for SQL injection and XXE. The D3 findings catalogue is much too narrow, covering only SQLi, JWT confusion, and XXE while leaving out MD5, hardcoded secret, no expiry, XSS, open redirect, path traversal, and cookie flags. D3 also introduces an unsupported 124,000,000 Naira exposure figure that does not trace to the exfil sample or to its own D2 math, so I applied the fabrication penalty and did not round the score up. D4 gives a practical ethical stance on journalists, internal evidence, scapegoating, and launch pressure, and it cites ISC2 Canon 1 and NDPA section 40. It should also cite ISC2 Canon 2 or 3 more directly, state the 72-hour NDPC deadline, and name section 41 for notifying high-risk affected data subjects. The single most important fix is to keep D3's business impact consistent with the evidence-backed sample calculation and carry the full D1 finding set into the final report.

name: Samuel Tobi Ogunnusi
feedback: D1 is concise and evidence-based, with solid coverage of SQL injection, alg:none, hardcoded JWT secret, missing exp and nbf, XXE, stored XSS, and open redirect. It misses unsalted MD5 password hashing, path traversal as its own finding, and the missing Secure and SameSite cookie controls. The decoy discussion partially understands that the signing function is not the real flaw, but it does not fully explain the Base64URL helper or the hash_equals constant-time comparison that make the safe construct safe. D2 gives a clean chain from SQL injection to dashboard access, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, and customer-data exposure, with CVSS vectors for the findings it includes. It omits recon, the failed login, JWT alg:none abuse, XXE, and the direct users.php timestamp, and the Naira impact remains at the broad tens-of-millions level rather than a sample-based estimate. D3 is a clear, usable report with an executive summary, threat model, findings, remediation order by risk per hour, and two detection stopgaps with false-positive notes. It loses credit because it carries only six findings, gives bare CVSS scores for some items, and does not include MD5, cookie flags, or path traversal in the final findings. D4 answers the journalist, documentation, colleague-evidence, and management-pressure parts well, and it ties the stance to ISC2 Canons I and II and the confirmed 312 affected customers. It should cite NDPA section 40 with the 72-hour NDPC duty and section 41 for affected high-risk data subjects. The single most important fix is to expand the D1 and D3 finding set to include MD5, path traversal, cookie flags, and the full safe-decoy explanation.

name: ayodeji oyesode
feedback: D1 is excellent, with the full core catalogue present: SQL injection, alg:none, no expiry, hardcoded secret, MD5, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, Secure, and SameSite. The evidence is specific and the explanations are technically grounded, especially around separating XXE from path traversal and treating MD5 as independent of SQL injection. D1 loses only a little credit because the decoy discussion focuses on the Base64URL helpers but does not also discuss the safe hash_equals HS256 comparison. D2 is a strong exploit-chain reconstruction, with SQLi, JWT forgery, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, and users.php exfiltration tied to PoCs, capture times, and what each hop enables. The CVSS table and highest-severity justification are strong, and the Naira estimate is sample-based, though the NDPA notification reference incorrectly names NITDA rather than the NDPC. D3 has a crisp executive headline, a useful threat model, evidence-tied findings, a real exploit chain, a risk-per-hour remediation order, and two specific detection stopgaps with false-positive expectations. D3 should carry the whole D1 catalogue into the report, since MD5, cookie flags, and path traversal are less visible there than in D1. D4 handles the journalist and colleague-evidence pressure well, and it correctly cites NDPA section 40 and the 72-hour notification duty. It should also say that verified technical facts do belong in the internal incident record, and it should cite section 41 for affected high-risk data subjects. The single most important fix is to bring the full D1 finding set and the hash_equals decoy detail into D3 and D4 instead of leaving them mostly in D1.

name: ASIA OLOLADE LADOKUN
feedback: D1 is methodical and evidence-led, with strong coverage of SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, the hardcoded JWT secret, missing expiry, cookie flags, open redirect, stored XSS, and XXE. It misses path traversal as a separate finding, and the decoy analysis correctly clears the Base64URL helpers but does not address the safe hash_equals HS256 comparison. D2 gives a coherent chain from SQL injection to JWT abuse, XXE, and customer-data exposure, with complete vectors for several key findings. It omits recon, the failed password attempt, stored XSS, open redirect, and path traversal, and the business impact underuses the sample because it only reports the visible sample balance total rather than extrapolating the 312-row exposure or giving the accepted tens-of-millions estimate. D3 is a polished report with a clear threat model, evidence-tied findings, a defensible statement that a precise financial-loss estimate cannot be supported, and practical SQLi and XXE detection stopgaps with false-positive rates. D3 remains too narrow because it centers SQLi, JWT, XXE, and exfiltration while leaving out several findings that were present in D1. D4 answers the journalist question, what goes into writing, how to preserve colleague-related evidence, and what action to take under management pressure. It cites ISC2 Canons I and II meaningfully and names the duty to notify the Commission and affected data subjects, but it should cite NDPA section 40, the 72-hour NDPC deadline, and section 41 explicitly. The single most important fix is to carry path traversal, XSS, open redirect, MD5, and cookie flags into D2 and D3 instead of compressing the attack to SQLi, JWT, and XXE.

name: Adegbile Mariam
feedback: D1 contains some real work, especially SQL injection, alg:none, XXE, insecure cookie handling, and a good explanation of why hash_equals is safe against timing attacks. It remains mostly template-shaped and misses MD5 as its own finding, the hardcoded JWT secret, missing exp and nbf as a separate lifecycle issue, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, and SameSite. D2 reconstructs a minimal chain of SQLi to JWT bypass to XXE and user data, and it gives CVSS vectors for those three findings. It skips recon, the failed login, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, and the exact users.php timeline, and it relies on a projected 49,467,600 NGN figure without enough sample math to support confidence in the calculation. D3 has the required sections in outline form, including executive summary, threat model, findings, decoy, exploit chain, business impact, remediation order, and detection stopgaps. The report is too thin for the management-report row because it only carries three findings, leaves several sections as template-like fragments, and does not give the two detection rules the level of concrete field and pattern detail expected. D4 speaks to pressure, truthful writing, colleague evidence, and decommissioning the server, and it cites ISC2 Canon 1. It misses the journalist-specific prompt, does not cite NDPA section 40, section 41, or the 72-hour NDPC requirement, and does not anchor the legal duty tightly enough to the 312 affected data subjects. I looked for a defensible way to push this higher, but the missing findings, template residue, thin chain, and incomplete ethics citations keep it below the next band. The single most important fix is to replace the template skeleton with a complete evidence-led catalogue and carry those findings through D2 and D3.

name: Oluwagbohunmi Ifeoluwa
flagReason: D2 and D3 invent a backup-file exfiltration path, a 02:25:14 download event, employee-style sample rows, a GRIOT attribution, and concrete 10,000,000 Naira fine or 14,097,232.34 Naira total-risk figures not supported by the evidence pack.
feedback: D1 is strong and covers the ten expected vulnerability areas with useful evidence: SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, cookie flags, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, and XXE. The Base64URL decoy explanation is also good, although it should additionally discuss the safe hash_equals comparison in the HS256 branch. D2 has many correct finding labels and several plausible CVSS vectors, but the exploit chain departs from the evidence pack in serious ways. It invents a /var/www/backup/05-exfil-sample.csv path, a 02:25:14 file download event, employee-style rows such as Kwame Mensah and Ama Serwaa, and a story that the hardcoded secret was discovered through file read before token forgery. D2 also turns the sample-balance total plus an unsupported 10,000,000 Naira fine into a concrete 14,097,232.34 Naira total-risk figure, so I applied the fabrication penalty and did not round the score up. D3 repeats the same fabricated backup-file path, GRIOT attribution, internal microservice blast radius, government fine, and shutdown claims, even though its remediation order and detection ideas are otherwise readable. D3 also uses the wrong decoy, clearing a supposed no-session log issue instead of the Base64URL or hash_equals construct. D4 answers the journalist, writing, colleague-evidence, and regulatory-notification pressure well, and it correctly names the NDPC 72-hour duty and affected data subjects. D4 still repeats the unsupported 14,097,232.34 Naira impact and needs section 40 and section 41 citations by number. The single most important fix is to remove invented paths, log events, people, fines, and totals, then rebuild D2 and D3 strictly from the provided capture, XML, token, and exfil sample.

name: Hamza Hashim
feedback: D1 is near model-answer quality, with the ten expected findings present and tied to the pack: SQL injection, unsalted MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing token lifecycle controls, stored XSS, XXE, path traversal, open redirect, and missing Secure and SameSite. The decoy work is especially good because it identifies the HS256 hash_equals comparison as safe and separates that constant-time comparison from the real alg:none and hardcoded-secret problems. D2 reconstructs the attack in strong chronological detail, including recon, failed guessing, SQLi, user enumeration, forged JWTs, stored XSS, open redirect, file read, XXE, exfiltration, CVSS vectors, and a sample-based Naira estimate. D2 loses only small credit because it slightly overstates cookie theft from the stored XSS despite the HttpOnly setting and uses a generic CVE-class reference where the local evidence should carry the argument. D3 is a polished management report with a clear threat model, evidence-led findings, the disproved decoy, exploit-chain breakpoints, effort-to-risk remediation, and exact detection logic with false-positive expectations. D3 could be even cleaner by keeping the regulatory wording to the NDPC rather than older or generic authority language. D4 is thoughtful, specific to the 312 affected customers, and answers the journalist, written record, colleague-evidence, and manager-pressure scenario in a recognisably personal voice. It loses marks because it cites the ISC2 honesty duty as Canon 3 instead of Canon II, and it does not cite NDPA section 40, the 72-hour NDPC deadline, and section 41 by number. This is comfortably in the top band because the technical work is complete and well evidenced. The single most important fix is to make the ethics citations as precise as the technical analysis.

name: Thapelo Seny Nyapele
feedback: D1 is strong and evidence-led, covering SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, cookie weakness, open redirect, stored XSS, and XXE. It misses path traversal as a separate catalogue finding, and some rows would be stronger with direct source or capture quotes rather than broader explanation. The decoy analysis is correct and useful because it clears the HS256 hash_equals comparison and identifies alg:none, the hardcoded secret, and missing expiry as the real JWT defects. D2 gives a very good chain from SQL injection through dashboard access, JWT forgery, users.php access, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, and the 312-record export. It has complete CVSS vectors and a defensible NGN 69.9 million estimate, but it does not include the initial recon and failed login steps and it treats a few hops more as separate events than as a tightly reconciled chain. D3 is a polished final report with a jargon-light headline, threat model, evidence-tied findings, the safe-decoy explanation, remediation priorities, and practical detection ideas. D3 loses credit mainly because the catalogue is not quite complete and the earliest-break argument could be sharper about fixing SQLi first while disabling alg:none and file-read paths immediately. D4 answers all four ethics prompts in a measured way and anchors the decision to the confirmed exposure of 312 customer records. It cites ISC2 Canons I and II and names the NDPC notification duty, but it should cite NDPA section 40 with the 72-hour deadline and section 41 for high-risk data-subject notification. The single most important fix is to add path traversal to D1 and carry that same complete ten-finding catalogue consistently through D2 and D3.

name: Durvesh Chandrakant Patil
feedback: D1 has a solid method and captures many important findings, including SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, cookie flags, open redirect, username enumeration, and XXE. It misses stored XSS and path traversal as standalone catalogue findings, and the client-controlled role row is really a consequence of the alg:none and hardcoded-secret issues rather than an independent answer-key item. The decoy section is correct because it explains that the HS256 branch recomputes the HMAC and compares it with hash_equals, so the real issue is the alg:none branch. D2 reconstructs a useful chain with SQLi, customer access, JWT weakness, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, and path traversal, and it includes CVSS vectors for the major findings. It loses marks for not fully preserving the expected timeline with recon and failed guessing, and for leaving the business impact at 312 affected customers without a sample-based Naira estimate. D3 is well structured and usable, with an executive summary, threat model, findings, decoy analysis, remediation plan, and detection ideas. D3 remains lighter than the strongest reports because it does not carry all ten findings, the customer-and-Naira headline is incomplete, and the detection stopgaps need more exact field and pattern detail plus false-positive rates. D4 answers the journalist, written-evidence, colleague, and manager-pressure questions responsibly, and it cites ISC2 Canons I and II in a load-bearing way. It names NDPA 2023 and the NDPC duty but should cite section 40, the 72-hour deadline, and section 41 explicitly. The single most important fix is to add the missing stored XSS, path traversal, and Naira-impact evidence throughout D1, D2, and D3.

name: ADEPOJU ESTHER
feedback: D1 shows good engagement with the evidence pack and identifies several real issues, including SQL injection, MD5, open redirect, stored XSS, path traversal, XXE, and customer PII exposure. The catalogue is uneven because the MD5, alg:none, and XXE rows have mismatched evidence in places, SQL injection is duplicated, and the hardcoded secret, missing exp and nbf controls, and missing Secure and SameSite cookie attributes are not clearly scored as their own findings. The decoy section is one of the stronger parts of D1 because it correctly clears the HS256 hash_equals comparison and points back to alg:none as the exploitable branch. D2 is much stronger than D1, with a coherent exploit chain, CVSS treatment, the 312-customer exposure, and a defensible sample-based estimate around NGN 63 million. It still loses credit for not making every expected hop and artifact line as explicit as the answer key, especially the initial recon and failed-login setup. D3 is a strong final report, with a customer-and-Naira headline, threat model, evidence-tied findings, a correct decoy discussion, remediation ordering by risk reduction, and exact detection patterns for alg:none and suspicious file reads. D3 should make the earliest-break fix more explicit and avoid relying on impact language that sounds broader than the confirmed evidence. D4 is excellent in practical stance: it answers the journalist, written record, colleague-evidence, and manager-pressure prompts, cites ISC2 Canons I and II, and ties the action to 312 customers and NDPA section 40 with a 72-hour NDPC clock. It only needs section 41 by number for high-risk affected data-subject notification. The single most important fix is to clean up D1 so each of the ten expected findings has the right evidence attached once, without duplicates or mismatched rows.

name: Somfechukwu Okany
flagReason: D1, D2, and D3 repeatedly invent out-of-pack SSRF, cloud metadata, IAM token theft, 50,000-customer exposure, billions of Naira exposure, and a sanitize_input decoy that are not in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 cannot receive technical credit because it is built around evidence that is not in the Stage 2 pack, including UNION extraction of IAM tokens, reflected XSS in a search box, stored XSS in notes, SSRF in an import function, cloud metadata access, and a sanitize_input decoy. The real D1 answer needed the legacy-admin SQL injection, unsalted MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing token expiry, stored comments XSS, XXE, path traversal, open redirect, cookie flags, and the safe Base64URL or hash_equals construct. D2 repeats the same out-of-pack story by claiming SQLi gave IAM tokens, SSRF reached the metadata service, and exfiltration involved roughly 50,000 customers and billions of Naira. Those claims do not trace to the capture, token file, XML payload, or 05-exfil-sample.csv, so I scored the affected D2 row at zero and applied the fabrication penalty. D3 again presents the fabricated SSRF and cloud-compromise chain, plus unsupported business impact figures such as 50,000 customers and billions of Naira. It does have the shape of a management report, but the evidence base is not the Sankofa pack being graded, so it cannot earn the technical report points. D4 is the only section with some standalone credit because it answers the journalist, written-record, evidence-preservation, and regulator-escalation themes in a practical way. D4 still cites the ISC2 canons with the numbers reversed and cites NDPA section 32 instead of section 40 and section 41. I looked for a defensible way to preserve more marks, but the central technical narrative relies on invented artefacts rather than the supplied evidence. The single most important fix is to discard the SSRF, IAM, metadata, 50,000-customer, and sanitize_input material and rebuild every deliverable from the actual Stage 2 artefacts.

name: Amna Zafar
feedback: D1 is strong and covers the expected vulnerability set, including SQL injection, MD5 without salt, alg:none, hardcoded JWT secret, missing expiry controls, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, and insecure cookie configuration. The hash_equals decoy is correctly handled as a false positive, with the real JWT issues identified as alg:none, hardcoded secret, and missing expiry. D1 loses only a little credit because the method section is thin, some CWE choices are approximate, and one authentication-bypass row duplicates the SQL injection finding rather than adding a new issue. D2 reconstructs a good chain from SQLi to users.php access, JWT forgery, stored XSS, open redirect, file read, XXE, and the 312-record export. It gives complete CVSS-style vectors and a defensible NGN 63M to NGN 77M exposure range, but it omits the initial recon and failed login steps and does not justify every CVSS vector in prose. D3 is a usable management report with an executive summary, threat model, evidence-tied findings, correct decoy discussion, chain, remediation order by exploit speed and implementation effort, and detection stopgaps. D3 loses credit for not ending the executive summary with a clear customers-and-Naira headline and for treating some items, such as cookie flags and open redirect, more as supporting issues than full findings. D4 is much thinner than the technical work: it gives a reasonable journalist response and says to escalate the breach under NDPA section 40, but it barely answers the written-record and colleague-evidence prompts. D4 cites ISC2 Canon 1 but misses section 41 and the explicit 72-hour NDPC deadline. The single most important fix is to bring the same precision from D1 into D4, especially the four ethics prompts and exact NDPA sections.

name: Enyi Jerry
feedback: Enyi, you submitted three of the four deliverables (D1 findings, D3 report, D4 ethics), and I graded each of those on its own merits. Your D1 findings catalogue is the strongest part of the work: you cleanly nailed the SQL injection via string concatenation in the login query, the unsalted MD5 password hashing, the JWT alg:none acceptance, the unvalidated open redirect through the ?next parameter, and the session cookie missing its Secure flag, each with a real evidence line and a sensible OWASP and CWE pairing. Where D1 lost ground is that you logged a reflected XSS row tied to the error message rather than the stored XSS beacon at 02:18:47 that the engagement actually contained, your hardcoded-secret reasoning got tangled together with the HS256 verification path, and three genuine findings never appear at all: the missing token expiry, the XXE reading file:///etc/passwd, and the path traversal that pulled root:x:0:0 at 02:24:02. A couple of your rows are also duplicates of the same SQLi or restate the same session issue, so they padded the count without adding a distinct finding. Your D3 report shows you understood the business stakes, since the executive summary names the 312 affected customers, the roughly 10 million naira exposure, and the six-week BoltCash runway, but the two highest-weight parts of that deliverable, the effort-ordered remediation roadmap and the two detection stopgaps, were left as the bracketed template placeholders with no real fixes, no field or pattern names, and no false-positive estimates, so I could only credit the framing you actually wrote. Your D4 answered just one of the four ethics prompts and cited ISC2 canons 2 and 4 by number, which is good instinct, but it stopped short of the NDPA 2023 specifics (section 40 with the NDPC 72-hour clock and section 41 on data subjects) and the text carried OCR-style garbling that made it read as a rough draft. I want to be clear and fair about the gaps: D2, the exploit chain and CVSS scoring, was not in your folder at all, so it scored zero, and the unfinished placeholder portions of D3 and the three unanswered D4 prompts could not earn credit because there was nothing there to assess, not because I doubted you. None of this is a fabrication issue; the evidence you did cite lines up with the real artefacts, so there is no penalty, just unfinished work. The single most important next step is to build out the missing D2 exploit chain with the timestamped attacker timeline and a justified CVSS vector for the SQLi, since that deliverable is worth 35 points and is currently a clean zero that is fully recoverable.
missingPieces: D2 exploit chain and CVSS (entire deliverable, scored 0). D3 remediation roadmap and both detection stopgaps left as empty template placeholders. D1 missing: token expiry CWE-613, XXE CWE-611, path traversal CWE-22; stored XSS logged as wrong instance. D4 only 1 of 4 prompts answered; no NDPA s40/s41/72h specifics.

name: Momina Noor
feedback: D1 has a real evidence-based core, with SQL injection, MD5 password hashing, alg:none, stored XSS, hardcoded JWT secret, path traversal, XXE, and the 312-record exposure discussed. It misses open redirect, missing exp and nbf controls, and missing Secure and SameSite cookie flags as proper standalone findings, and it duplicates MD5 while treating business impact as a vulnerability row. The hardcoded secret is explained correctly in prose, although the table mangles the string, and the decoy credit is partial because it clears the Base64URL helpers but not the safe hash_equals comparison. D2 gives a readable chain for SQL injection, users.php access, path traversal, XXE, and final data exposure. It leaves out recon, failed login, JWT abuse as a real hop, stored XSS, and open redirect, and the CVSS table uses incomplete vector placeholders rather than complete CVSS vectors. The Naira impact is at least stated, but the NGN 15.6 million estimate is based on an assumed NGN 50,000 per customer rather than the sample balance calculation expected by the brief. D3 has a clear executive summary, threat model, decoy explanation, chain, remediation order by effort and risk, and two practical detection ideas. It loses substantial credit because it does not provide a full findings section tied to evidence, carries only a subset of the ten issues, and repeats the low-support NGN 15.6 million estimate. D4 is practical and personal, answers all four pressure points, cites ISC2 Canons I and II, and names the 72-hour NDPC duty, but it should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number and avoid calling the affected people administrative dashboard users. The single most important fix is to complete the missing findings and replace the placeholder CVSS and impact math with exact vectors and sample-based Naira calculations.

name: courage tuedor
flagReason: D2 and D3 introduce unsupported potential-impact figures of over 2.1 billion Naira that do not trace to the 05-exfil-sample.csv calculation or the evidence pack.
feedback: D1 has a good method section and correctly identifies SQL injection, alg:none, hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, open redirect, MD5, XXE, and path traversal. It misses stored XSS and the missing Secure and SameSite cookie attributes, and the decoy answer is wrong because it treats the hand-rolled JWT functions as exploitable rather than proving the safe Base64URL helper or hash_equals comparison. D2 gives a readable chain for SQLi, JWT forgery, XXE or file read, and data exfiltration, with useful PoCs and several complete CVSS vectors. It omits the failed login, stored XSS, open redirect as an actual hop, and a clean separation between XXE and path traversal. D2 also introduces an unsupported over-2.1-billion-Naira potential-impact figure, while the defensible sample-based direct exposure it gives is about 56 million Naira, so I applied the fabrication penalty and did not round the score up. D3 has an executive summary, threat model, selected findings, remediation priorities, and deployable detection stopgaps. D3 loses credit for carrying only a subset of the ten findings, repeating the wrong decoy, and repeating the unsupported 2.1 billion Naira impact figure. D4 is much stronger, with a clear journalist stance, factual written-record stance, colleague-evidence handling, and NDPC notification escalation for the 312 affected customers. It should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number, but the ethical reasoning is otherwise practical and anchored to the work. The single most important fix is to replace the inflated impact claim and wrong decoy with the evidence-backed Naira calculation and the safe hash_equals or Base64URL analysis.

name: Syed Azlan Shah
feedback: D1 is concise and technically clean on the items it includes: SQL injection, alg:none, hardcoded credentials, XXE, path traversal, stored XSS, insecure cookie transport, and the safe hash_equals decoy. It misses unsalted MD5, missing exp and nbf token lifetime controls, open redirect, and SameSite as a distinct cookie issue, so the catalogue is not complete. The decoy explanation is a strength because it correctly says hash_equals is constant-time and the real JWT flaw is the alg:none fallback. D2 gives a compact exploit chain for SQLi, JWT alg:none, path traversal, and PII exfiltration, with working PoCs and a sound sample-based estimate of about 63 million Naira. It omits recon, failed credential guessing, stored XSS, open redirect, and a separate XXE hop, and the CVSS table groups findings too aggressively rather than scoring each answer-key finding. D3 is crisp and business-facing, with a good customer-and-Naira headline, a threat model, the disproved decoy, a chain, remediation by effort, and two concrete stopgaps. D3 is limited by the same narrow findings set, since the final report does not carry MD5, missing expiry, open redirect, stored XSS, and cookie issues through as full findings. D4 handles the journalist, written record, colleague evidence, and manager-pressure question well, and cites ISC2 Canon II and NDPA section 40 with the 72-hour NDPC clock. It should also cite ISC2 Canon I for the public-interest duty and NDPA section 41 for affected high-risk data subjects. The single most important fix is to expand the compact report into the full ten-finding catalogue instead of focusing mainly on SQLi, JWT, and file disclosure.

name: Julian Emonfomwan
flagReason: D1, D2, and D3 invent a UNION extraction of IAM tokens, SSRF to AWS metadata, cloud infrastructure compromise, and AWS IMDS remediation that are not in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 cannot receive technical credit because it changes the evidence pack into a different incident, claiming a UNION payload that extracts IAM tokens, SSRF to cloud metadata, and infrastructure compromise. The real D1 findings should have been the Sankofa SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing token expiry, stored comments XSS, XXE, path traversal, open redirect, cookie flags, and the safe Base64URL or hash_equals decoy. D2 repeats the fabricated IAM-token and AWS metadata chain, including an import feature reaching 169.254.169.254, which is not in the supplied artefacts. Because that invented chain is the backbone of the deliverable, I scored the affected D2 row at zero and applied the fabrication penalty. D3 again frames the breach as AWS cloud infrastructure escalation and recommends IMDSv2 and egress filtering as if SSRF were proven in this pack. The management report has a professional tone, but its central evidence does not match the Stage 2 answer key. D4 is substantially better because it gives a proper journalist refusal, a factual written-record stance, a colleague-evidence stance, and an escalation action for breach notification. It cites ISC2 Canon II and the 72-hour NDPC duty, but it should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number and avoid relying on the fabricated cloud narrative. I looked for a defensible way to preserve more marks, but the technical deliverables are dominated by out-of-pack evidence. The single most important fix is to remove the IAM, SSRF, AWS metadata, and IMDS material and rebuild the capstone from the actual capture, token, XML, and exfil sample files.

name: Jephta Adegbola
feedback: D1 has a useful method and correctly discusses MD5 without salt, alg:none, XXE, SQL injection, and customer PII exposure. It is far short of the full catalogue because it misses the hardcoded JWT secret as a scored row, missing exp and nbf as a row, stored XSS, path traversal, open redirect, cookie flags, and the actual safe decoy. Some evidence labels are also off, such as calling the XML file a token artefact and using the wrong OWASP class for SQL injection. D2 is much stronger, with recon, failed login, SQL injection, JWT abuse, XXE, file disclosure, and exfiltration described in order with timestamps and artefact excerpts. It loses marks because stored XSS and open redirect are not developed as chain hops, the CVSS vectors are mostly absent, and the Naira impact is intentionally left unquantified beyond customers and data class. D3 is a thoughtful management report with a clear summary, threat model, chain, earliest break at SQL injection, effort-aware remediation, and two concrete detection stopgaps. D3 loses credit for naming the open redirect as the decoy instead of Base64URL or hash_equals, carrying only a partial findings set, and overstating the impact as hundreds of millions of Naira without a sample-based calculation. D4 answers the journalist, writing, colleague-evidence, and manager-pressure prompts in a mature voice. It does not cite an ISC2 canon by number and does not cite NDPA section 40, section 41, or the 72-hour deadline explicitly, even though it names the NDPC and affected-customer notification duty. The single most important fix is to rebuild D1 around all ten answer-key findings and then add complete CVSS vectors to D2.

name: shaffi Ibrahim-ikoko
flagReason: D2 and D3 introduce unsupported 200 million to 500 million Naira impact figures that do not trace to the exfil sample or the provided business evidence.
feedback: D1 has a useful narrative method and solid evidence for SQL injection, alg:none, missing token expiry, hardcoded JWT secret, XXE, stored XSS, and path traversal. It misses unsalted MD5 as its own finding, open redirect as its own finding, and the missing Secure and SameSite cookie attributes. The decoy answer is partially right because it explains Base64URL and HMAC verification are not the real bugs, but it does not name hash_equals as the constant-time safe comparison clearly enough. D2 reconstructs a strong practical chain with recon, failed login, SQLi, JWT forgery, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, and exfiltration. The CVSS section is present, but the Naira impact invents a 200 million to 500 million combined exposure that is not traceable to the sample or business artefacts, so I applied the fabrication penalty and did not round the score up. D3 is much too thin for the report deliverable, with a short executive summary, a few bullets, and a note that a full DOCX exists elsewhere rather than the full report content being present in the submitted text. D3 also repeats the unsupported 200 million to 500 million Naira exposure. D4 gives a human journalist stance and says to preserve factual evidence and escalate breach notification, but it cites NDPA section 24 instead of section 40 and section 41. It also does not fully answer the senior-colleague evidence prompt with the precision expected. The single most important fix is to submit the full D3 report content and keep all Naira impact to the evidence-backed 312-customer sample calculation.

name: Daniel Bolaji-Busola
flagReason: D1, D2, D3, and D4 introduce unsupported SSRF to AWS metadata and IAM credential exposure that are not in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 is otherwise one of the stronger catalogues, with SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, missing expiry, hardcoded secret, open redirect, cookie flags, stored XSS, XXE, path traversal, customer exposure, and the Base64URL decoy all discussed with evidence. It loses credit because it adds an unsupported SSRF to AWS metadata finding and treats it as confirmed, which is not part of the Stage 2 evidence pack. D2 has a clear chain for SQL injection, stored XSS, path traversal, XXE, JWT issues, and customer exfiltration, plus a defensible 312-customer and 57.4 million Naira calculation. However, D2 makes SSRF to cloud metadata a major hop, gives an AWS metadata PoC, and discusses IAM role exposure even while saying response content was not captured, so the fabricated cloud row is zeroed and the penalty is applied. D3 is polished and management-ready in tone, with a good headline, threat model, remediation priorities, sample-based impact, and concrete stopgaps. D3 still repeats the SSRF and AWS metadata story in findings, chain, remediation, and detection, which materially changes the incident. D4 is strong on the journalist refusal, written record, colleague evidence, and non-negotiable NDPC/customer notification stance, and it cites ISC2 Canons I and II. It should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number, and it should not anchor the ethics narrative to the unsupported SSRF finding. This would have been a high-scoring report without the cloud-metadata material. The single most important fix is to remove the SSRF and IAM claims and keep the chain to SQLi, JWT, XSS, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, and the 312-row export.

name: OPEYEMI KAYODE
feedback: D1 is very well written and explains most findings in plain English with strong evidence, including SQL injection, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, open redirect, cookie flags, MD5, XXE, and the safe hash_equals decoy. It loses credit because the XSS row is framed as reflected XSS in the login error rather than the required stored comments XSS, and path traversal is folded into the XXE discussion rather than scored as its own finding. The decoy section is excellent, because it explains exactly why hash_equals is safe and distinguishes it from alg:none and the hardcoded secret. D2 is excellent, with recon, failed login, SQLi, users.php access, JWT forgery, stored XSS, open redirect, direct path traversal, XXE, exfiltration, complete chain scoring, and sample-based Naira impact around 63 million. D2 also handles assumptions responsibly by refusing to invent NDPA fines or BoltCash revenue impact without inputs. D3 is a strong management report, with a plain-English executive summary, threat model, findings tied to evidence, decoy proof, full chain, remediation ranked by risk reduction per hour, and precise detection stopgaps with false-positive expectations. D3 earns a high score even though it inherits the D1 issue of calling one XSS reflected and treating some chain-level items more clearly than the D1 table did. D4 answers all four ethical prompts in a direct voice and cites ISC2 Canons 1 and 2. It correctly cites NDPA section 40 and the 72-hour NDPC duty, although the affected-customer notification should be cited as section 41 rather than section 40(3). The single most important fix is to make D1 match the answer key exactly by adding stored comments XSS and direct path traversal as separate findings.

name: Richard Afolabi
flagReason: D1, D2, and D3 invent exposed backup.sql, mysql-general.log UNION IAM-token extraction, SSRF to cloud metadata, and IAM credential exposure that are not in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 contains some real answer-key material, including SQL injection, stored XSS, alg:none, XXE, hardcoded secret, cookie flags, MD5, missing expiry, path traversal, open redirect, and a Base64URL decoy. The problem is that it is mixed with major out-of-pack findings: exposed backup.sql, mysql-general.log UNION extraction of iam_token, SSRF to 169.254.169.254, and cloud IAM credential exposure. Those invented findings materially change the incident, so the affected technical rows lose credit and I applied the fabrication penalty. D2 is built around the same unsupported backup-file, UNION IAM-token, and SSRF-to-cloud-metadata chain, so it cannot earn normal exploit-chain credit even though it mentions some real Sankofa concepts. D2 does correctly name 312 affected customers and gives a cautious tens-of-millions impact statement, but that cannot rescue a chain whose first hops are not in the evidence pack. D3 again centres backup.sql, mysql logs, SSRF, and cloud credentials, and even uses incomplete placeholder CVSS vectors. The Base64URL decoy discussion is reasonable, but most of the management report is aimed at the wrong incident. D4 has a proper instinct to avoid journalist disclosure and preserve evidence, and it cites ISC2 Canon 1 in support of reporting. It is too short and does not fully answer the written-record or senior-colleague prompts, nor does it cite NDPA section 40, section 41, or the 72-hour NDPC duty. The single most important fix is to remove backup.sql, mysql-general.log, IAM-token, SSRF, and cloud metadata claims, then rebuild D2 and D3 from the actual Stage 2 artefacts.

name: Daniel Lawal
feedback: D1 is a solid catalogue with clear evidence for SQL injection, unsalted MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing token expiry, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, cookie flags, and the hash_equals decoy. It misses stored XSS as a standalone finding, which is why it cannot reach the top D1 band. The decoy explanation is good because it correctly says hash_equals performs constant-time comparison and the real issue is elsewhere. D2 reconstructs recon, SQLi, users.php access, file disclosure, XXE, and customer-data exfiltration with useful PoCs. It loses marks because it omits the failed login, JWT abuse, stored XSS, and open redirect as chain hops, and the CVSS table covers only part of the finding set. The business impact names 312 records and gives the average balance, but it does not multiply that into a clear projected Naira total. D3 is readable and has an executive summary, threat model, findings categories, decoy verdict, chain, remediation order, and two stopgaps. D3 is still fairly compressed, does not end with a customers-and-Naira headline, and the detection stopgaps lack exact false-positive expectations. D4 answers the main ethical questions and cites ISC2 Canons 1 and 2, but it only refers to NDPA notification generally and does not cite section 40, section 41, or the 72-hour NDPC clock. The single most important fix is to add stored XSS throughout D1 to D3 and make the D2 chain and impact math complete.

name: Suzzie Ukpong
feedback: D1 is outstanding, with a complete evidence-led catalogue, correct OWASP and CWE mapping, separate treatment of cookie Secure and SameSite, strong method, and a precise hash_equals decoy explanation. It also distinguishes the safe HS256 comparison from the real alg:none and hardcoded-secret failures in a way engineering can act on. D2 is also excellent, reconstructing the chain from recon and failed login through SQLi, users.php access, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, token issues, and the 312-row exfiltration. The CVSS work is unusually complete and the sample-based NGN 63,027,625 exposure is well supported, though there is a little unnecessary side commentary about SSRF from the wider lab that should not be treated as a Stage 2 finding. D3 is a polished management report with a CFO-ready headline, threat model, full findings, disproved decoy, chain, risk-per-hour remediation, and exact detection stopgaps with false-positive expectations. It earns near-full credit because it carries the evidence and business logic consistently across the report. D4 is thoughtful and brave on the journalist, written record, colleague evidence, and notification-pressure prompts. It cites ISC2 Canons I, II, and III, and names a 72-hour NDPC notification duty, but it cites NDPA section 2.6 rather than section 40 and section 41. This is a top-band report with only small legal precision issues. The single most important fix is to correct the NDPA citations in D4 and keep any SSRF lab references out of the Stage 2 findings.

name: Abeiku Quayson
feedback: D1 is strong and nearly complete, with SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, client-controlled role claims, cookie flags, open redirect, stored XSS, path traversal, XXE, customer exposure, and a good hash_equals decoy. The extra role-claim and customer-exposure rows are consequences rather than separate answer-key findings, but they do not undermine the core catalogue. D2 is much weaker than D1 because the chain focuses on SQLi, dashboard access, users.php access, path traversal, and exfiltration while leaving out recon, the failed login, JWT abuse, stored XSS, and open redirect as real hops. The CVSS table uses placeholder strings like CVSS:3.1/AV/AC/PR/UI/S/C/I/A instead of complete vectors, so the CVSS row cannot receive full credit. D2 does include a reasonable business-impact estimate of about 68.4 million Naira, although the average balance appears higher than the expected sample average. D3 is a clear report with threat model, findings tied to evidence, Base64URL decoy, exploit-chain narrative, remediation order, and SQLi plus XXE or file-read detection stopgaps. It loses credit for not carrying the precise Naira estimate into the executive summary and for not making the JWT hop as concrete as D1 did. D4 answers all four pressure points in a mature way and cites ISC2 Canons I and II. It names the NDPA notification duty and the NDPC, but it should cite section 40, section 41, and the 72-hour deadline explicitly. The single most important fix is to replace the placeholder CVSS strings with complete vectors and make JWT, stored XSS, and open redirect part of the D2 chain.

name: Rwotolara Innocent
feedback: D1 has a sensible method and correctly identifies SQL injection, unsafe alg:none token handling, open redirect, stored XSS, path traversal, XXE, and data exposure. It misses unsalted MD5, the hardcoded JWT secret, missing exp and nbf controls, and the missing Secure and SameSite cookie attributes. The decoy answer is wrong because it treats the XXE entity as the suspicious construct and concludes it is exploitable, instead of disproving the safe Base64URL helper or hash_equals comparison. D2 gives a readable chain from SQL injection through token abuse, open redirect, file read or XXE, and data export. It leaves out recon and the failed login, does not develop stored XSS as a chain hop, and gives broad CVSS scores rather than complete vectors for each finding. D2 also names 312 affected customers but does not calculate a sample-based Naira exposure. D3 is structured and understandable, with an executive summary, threat model, findings, chain, remediation order, and two detection stopgaps. It repeats the wrong decoy, carries only a partial finding set, and still lacks the customers-and-Naira headline the brief expects. D4 is comparatively strong, with a clear journalist boundary, factual writing stance, colleague-evidence handling, and a non-negotiable 72-hour NDPC notification stance. It should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number, and D4 cannot make up for the missing technical catalogue. The single most important fix is to learn the real decoy and add the missing MD5, hardcoded secret, token expiry, and cookie findings.

name: Timothe ALOGNON
feedback: D1 is a broad and mostly correct findings catalogue. It identifies SQL injection, weak MD5 password hashing, the hardcoded JWT secret, alg:none acceptance, missing exp and nbf lifecycle controls, open redirect, stored XSS, XXE, and a cookie Secure issue, and it correctly rejects the Base64URL helper as the decoy. It loses credit because the hardcoded secret and weak secret are split into overlapping findings, the cookie finding does not fully capture SameSite, the path traversal endpoint is not clearly separated from XXE, and username enumeration is extra rather than one of the expected ten rows. D2 reconstructs a plausible attack path with SQL injection, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE or file read, and the 312-row customer exposure. The CVSS section includes real vectors and the Naira estimate is close to the expected sample-based value at about 64 million Naira. The chain is not as precise as it should be because recon and the failed login are not carried as early steps, users.php access happened before the later XSS and redirect activity, and the report overstates what /etc/passwd would hand to the next hop. D3 has the main executive ingredients: a customer and Naira headline, threat model, substantiated findings, decoy, chain, remediation order, and two stopgaps. It loses marks for some imprecise severity reasoning, an odd claim that the attacker was from Berlin based on the Tor exit, and detection stopgaps that read more like input validation pseudocode than deployable log patterns with fields. D4 gives a sensible ethical stance, refuses the journalist, explains what should and should not be written, escalates colleague-relevant evidence, and cites ISC2 Canons I and II. It should cite NDPA 2023 section 40 and section 41 explicitly, name the NDPC, and distinguish regulatory notice from affected-customer notice. This was close enough to the next band that I looked for a humane round up, but the missing path traversal finding and weak detection specificity did not justify moving it higher.

name: Nwaka Ozioma
feedback: D1 is careful about method and correctly covers SQL injection, MD5 hashing, alg:none acceptance, hardcoded secret, missing token expiry, open redirect, insecure cookies, and username leak or possible XSS. The hash_equals decoy is very good because it focuses on the exact safe comparison and explains why the surrounding JWT design is still unsafe. The main problem is coverage: D1 does not clearly list stored XSS in comments, XXE, or path traversal as first-class findings, and it merges username leakage with possible XSS rather than separating answer-key issues from supporting observations. D2 is substantially stronger. It builds a chain from SQL injection to forged or weak JWT trust, XXE file read, users.php data access, and the 312-record export, with a complete CVSS table and a reasonable sample-based estimate of about 63 million Naira. It still misses the opening recon and failed login as chronology points, and stored XSS plus open redirect are not used as concrete chain steps even though the CVSS table mentions them. D3 is a readable client report with executive summary, threat model, findings, decoy, chain, remediation and detection content. It earns credit for being grounded and for not chasing hash_equals. It loses credit because the report inherits D1's incomplete finding set in places, the detection stopgaps are less exact than requested, and the customer-and-Naira headline could be sharper at the top. D4 is ethically sound but too short. It refuses the journalist, keeps writing to verified facts, treats colleague evidence fairly, and recognizes NDPA reporting and affected-customer notification. It cites ISC2 Canon I and mentions Section 40, but it does not give the 72-hour NDPC deadline clearly and does not cite section 41 by number. The mark is a solid pass, but the missing D1 findings keep it out of the higher range.

name: Oluwafisayomi Adekoya
flagReason: Unsupported AWS or Elasticsearch reachability, backup.sql and .env remediation, and external impact ceiling were presented without evidence from the capstone pack.
feedback: D1 is excellent. It finds almost the complete answer-key set: SQL injection, MD5 with no salt, JWT alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing exp and nbf, open redirect, stored XSS, path traversal, XXE, and missing Secure and SameSite cookie controls. It also treats the Base64URL helper as a decoy and explains that the real JWT failure sits nearby in jwt_verify. The only small deductions are for adding username enumeration as an extra finding and for being slightly cautious on stored XSS despite the submitted payload evidence. D2 is also strong. It gives the expected timestamps from recon through failed login, SQLi, users.php access, stored XSS, redirect, XXE or file read, and final exfiltration, includes full CVSS vectors, and calculates the 312-customer exposure from the 20-row sample at about 63 million Naira. It loses a little credit because the IBM per-record ceiling and additional regulatory-cost figures are outside the capstone evidence and should not be blended into the assessed business impact. D3 is one of the clearer executive reports in this batch, with a good customers-and-Naira opening, threat model, findings tied to artifacts, a disproved decoy, an exploit timeline, effort-to-risk remediation, and concrete detection patterns with false-positive expectations. The serious problem is that it adds unsupported infrastructure statements about AWS metadata reachability, Elasticsearch paths, backup.sql, and .env. Those claims were not in the evidence pack, so I applied the fabrication penalty and did not round the score upward. D4 is mature and well anchored to the work. It refuses the journalist, limits written material to verified report content, handles colleague-relevant evidence by preserving the artifact trail, and identifies NDPA section 40(2) and the 72-hour clock. It should also cite section 41 for affected high-risk data subjects, but the overall ethical reasoning is strong.

name: Umer Ashraf
flagReason: The report treats SSRF to AWS metadata, IAM credential exposure, full AWS compromise, and unsupported cost figures as confirmed evidence.
feedback: D1 identifies several important issues, including SQL injection, alg:none token handling, MD5 hashing, missing token expiry, hardcoded secret, and missing cookie flags, and it recognizes the Base64URL helper as a decoy. It is incomplete against the answer key because open redirect, stored XSS, path traversal, and XXE are not clearly presented as first-class D1 findings. Some rows also use weak or mismatched classifications, such as treating Base64URL as inadequate encryption before later calling it safe. D2 has a useful chronological walkthrough of recon, the failed login, SQL injection, users.php access, stored XSS, open redirect, and path traversal, with several full CVSS vectors. It loses substantial credit because it omits the expected Naira business-impact calculation, gives only a partial finding set in the CVSS section, and introduces SSRF as a scored finding even though the capstone evidence supports XXE and path traversal, not AWS metadata compromise. D3 is where the largest problem appears. The report has structure and includes an executive summary, threat model, findings, chain, CVSS, remediation, and detections, but it makes unsupported SSRF, AWS IAM credential theft, full AWS account compromise, GDPR exposure, and 2 to 5 million Naira remediation cost central to the story. That is a fabrication issue under this marking guide, so I applied the penalty and flagged it for senior review. The correct evidence would have supported SQL injection, JWT flaws, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, cookie flags, and 312 customer records, without the AWS layer. D4 answers the journalist and says evidence should go through official channels, and it gives a reasonable stance on not protecting or condemning a senior without evidence. It cites ISC2 Canon I, but it does not cite NDPA section 40, section 41, the NDPC 72-hour notification deadline, or affected high-risk data-subject notice. Because the report contains central unsupported compromise claims, I did not apply any humane upward rounding near the cutoff.

name: Praise olivia Mazana
flagReason: Unsupported SSRF to AWS metadata, IAM credential theft, full cloud compromise, and reflected-XSS simulator evidence are treated as part of the capstone facts.
feedback: D1 is close to complete. It covers SQL injection, unsalted MD5, JWT alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing exp and nbf, missing Secure and SameSite cookie controls, open redirect, XXE, stored XSS, and directory traversal. The hash_equals decoy is handled well: the report correctly says the constant-time HS256 comparison is not the exploitable part and separates it from alg:none. The main D1 deductions are for adding unsupported reflected-XSS simulator material and username enumeration as extra findings, plus a few line-number and severity imprecisions. D2 has the expected shape of an exploit chain and includes full CVSS vectors and a customer-and-Naira impact section. It earns credit for SQL injection, stored XSS, XXE or file read, users.php access, and 312 affected customers. It loses a lot because it leaves out the early recon and failed login, gets the chronology muddy by placing the 02:16 users.php export after later activity, overstates the sample-based exposure as about 68.1 million Naira, and treats SSRF to AWS metadata with IAM credential theft as confirmed when the evidence pack does not support that. D3 is a polished client-facing report with an executive headline, threat model, findings, decoy, chain, remediation order, and two detection stopgaps. However, the same unsupported SSRF/AWS compromise becomes central in D3, including a detection stopgap for metadata access and claims about full cloud compromise. That required a fabrication penalty and senior-review flag. D4 is strong. It refuses the journalist, confines writing to verified formal channels, preserves colleague-relevant evidence, names the NDPC, and recognizes affected data-subject notification. It should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 explicitly, but the ethical posture is grounded in the work. I considered whether the strong D1 and D4 justified a higher mark, but the AWS fabrication affects D2 and D3 too directly to round upward.

name: Mmesoma Blessing Egeonu
feedback: D1 captures several core issues: weak MD5 hashing, SQL injection, JWT alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing token expiry, insecure cookie flags, open redirect, and username disclosure. The Base64URL decoy answer is acceptable because it explains that the helper only converts data format and does not execute code. The catalogue is still materially incomplete because it does not list stored XSS or path traversal as D1 findings, treats the XML issue as a browser parsing error rather than XXE, and does not clearly mention SameSite on the cookie row. D2 is much stronger. It reconstructs discovery, SQL injection, users.php access, the 312-record export, stored XSS, open redirect, arbitrary file read, and JWT weaknesses. It includes CVSS vectors and calculates the business impact correctly at about 63.0 million Naira from the 20-row sample. It loses credit for hop numbering and sequencing, for not treating XXE correctly, and for making some chain handoffs sound speculative rather than evidence-led. D3 has a good executive summary with 312 customers and about 63 million Naira, a clear threat model, findings tied to evidence, a remediation section ordered around SQL injection first, and detection stopgaps for SQL injection and file-read attempts. It loses significant credit because it explicitly dismisses XXE as unsubstantiated even though the XML artifact is part of the answer key, and because the finding set is narrower than expected. D4 refuses the journalist, keeps written records to verified evidence, escalates colleague-relevant material properly, and recognizes NDPA notification plus affected-individual notice. It cites ISC2 Canons I and II, but it does not cite NDPA section 40, section 41, or the 72-hour NDPC deadline precisely. The score is a solid pass, but the incorrect XXE handling is the main thing holding it back.

name: Abdulsamad Babangida
feedback: D1 is excellent and earns full credit. It identifies the expected findings: SQL injection, unsalted MD5, JWT alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing exp and nbf, missing Secure and SameSite cookie controls, open redirect, stored XSS, path traversal, and XXE. It also adds the bulk PII exposure as a consequence, but the answer-key catalogue is still intact. The decoy section is especially strong because it distinguishes the broken alg:none branch from the safe HS256 branch protected by hash_equals. D2 is good but not as complete as D1. It includes full CVSS vectors for key findings, covers SQL injection, JWT alg:none, path traversal, XXE, stored XSS, and final PII exposure, and explains the sensitivity of 312 records. It loses credit because the PDF text shows an incomplete or reordered chain, the table omits several catalogue issues such as MD5, hardcoded secret, cookie flags, expiry, and open redirect, and the Naira impact is described only as tens of millions rather than carrying the expected sample-based estimate clearly. D3 is very strong. It gives Bayo a clear executive summary, a realistic threat model, substantiated findings, a precise hash_equals decoy, an exploit chain, CVSS and business-impact discussion, risk-per-hour remediation, and deployable SQLi plus alg:none detection stopgaps with low false-positive reasoning. It loses only small marks for some scope-change overstatement, for not using the exact Naira total, and for saying every vulnerability is present in BoltCash today more strongly than the evidence can prove. D4 is thoughtful and evidence-led: it refuses the journalist, limits writing to formal channels, preserves the complete timeline for Amaka, and treats the 312 customers as the public interest. It cites ISC2 Canons I and II and recognizes NDPC notification, but it does not cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number or state the 72-hour deadline explicitly. The work is comfortably in the high band.

name: Nicole Enyonam Agbanyo
flagReason: Unsupported exfiltration path, 68.5 million Naira total, customer-notification and legal-cost figures, BoltCash rebuild timelines, and infrastructure claims are presented as facts.
feedback: D1 is organized and evidence-aware. It correctly identifies SQL injection, JWT alg:none, missing exp and nbf, hardcoded secret, cookie Secure weakness, open redirect, XXE, directory traversal, and unsalted MD5. The Base64URL decoy is explained well. D1 loses credit because stored XSS is missing from the catalogue, the cookie finding does not fully surface SameSite as a separate control gap, and the report treats the alg:none token as definitely used in the wild rather than as evidence of an accepted vulnerable token. D2 has a readable five-hop chain and includes CVSS vectors plus a business-impact section. It covers recon, SQL injection, JWT manipulation, directory traversal, and exfiltration, but it omits stored XSS and open redirect as chain steps, invents or assumes an exfiltration path such as /var/www/legacy-admin/data/customers.csv, and gives a 68.5 million Naira total plus customer-notification, legal-fee, and rebuild-cost figures that are not traceable to the capstone sample. That is why I applied the fabrication penalty. D3 is polished and mostly actionable, with an executive summary, threat model, findings, decoy, remediation order, and detection stopgaps for SQL injection and alg:none. It is held back by the same unsupported cost and launch-planning claims, plus statements such as no WAF, plain HTTP in network segments, every vulnerability being present in BoltCash, and board-level rebuild timelines. The correct report should stay with the observed Sankofa evidence and the sample-based 312-customer impact. D4 is clear on refusing the journalist and preserving colleague-relevant evidence, and it anchors the action to NDPC notification. It cites ISC2 Canons I and II, but it cites section 41 as the Commission notification authority where the guide expected section 40 for NDPC notice and section 41 for affected high-risk data subjects. The answer also says not to hand evidence to Legal unvetted, which is riskier than the expected formal escalation posture. Because the unsupported figures affect both D2 and D3, there was no defensible reason to round this upward.

name: NATHALIE DIANE TCHOUMI MBIAMI
feedback: D1 is detailed and careful about evidence. It correctly identifies SQL injection, MD5 hashing, open redirect, JWT alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing exp and nbf, missing Secure, missing SameSite, and XXE, and it properly disproves the hash_equals comparison as the decoy. It loses credit because stored XSS and path traversal are not clearly listed as catalogue findings, while extra rows such as role trust and verbose username disclosure take space that should have gone to the answer-key findings. D2 reconstructs a coherent chain from SQL injection to JWT weakness, XXE file disclosure, and customer exposure. It includes CVSS vectors and a customer-and-Naira section. The deductions are for omitting the early failed-login step, not integrating stored XSS and open redirect as real attack-chain activity, folding the path traversal evidence into the exfiltration hop rather than scoring it cleanly, and using a 67.5 million Naira estimate instead of the expected sample-based value. D3 is stronger than D2 as a client report. It has a clear executive headline, threat model, substantiated findings, hash_equals decoy, exploit chain, business impact, remediation order, and practical SQLi and alg:none detection stopgaps. It loses credit because it ranks JWT ahead of SQL injection as the earliest break point, misses several catalogue details in the main findings list, and carries the same inflated Naira estimate. D4 is mature: it refuses the journalist, limits written material to verified facts, preserves colleague evidence, recognizes NDPC and affected-data-subject notification, and anchors the stance in ISC2 Canons I and II. It should cite NDPA section 40, section 41, and the 72-hour deadline explicitly. I looked for a defensible round up, but the missing D1 stored XSS and path traversal rows kept it below the next band.

name: Triumph Izegaegbe
flagReason: Unsupported regulatory fine, remediation cost, business-risk cost, and total financial-impact figures are presented without support from the capstone sample.
feedback: D1 covers much of the expected catalogue. It identifies SQL injection, hardcoded secret, missing exp and nbf, unsalted MD5, JWT alg:none, stored XSS, open redirect, missing Secure and SameSite cookie controls, and path traversal or arbitrary file read. The Base64URL decoy is handled correctly. D1 loses marks because XXE is not as clearly substantiated as a first-class catalogue row, some evidence is thin or repeated, and the extra wording around the Base64URL helper outputting into alg:none muddies an otherwise correct decoy answer. D2 reconstructs the attack from reconnaissance through SQL injection, session use, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE or file read, and exfiltration. The CVSS section has real vector strings for major findings, but the impact section is weak against the rubric: it names 312 customers yet does not calculate the sample-based Naira exposure, and instead introduces unsupported statutory penalties, remediation costs, and business-risk costs. D3 is a substantial report with executive summary, threat model, findings, decoy, remediation phases, and two deployable WAF detections. It loses credit because its business impact relies on unsupported 56 million Naira and 4.6 million Naira figures, its remediation ordering is less tied to the earliest chain break than expected, and it treats XXE as enabling SSRF/internal scanning beyond the evidence. D4 refuses the journalist, commits to factual writing, preserves evidence even where a senior admin may be implicated, and recognizes NDPC and affected-customer notification. It cites ISC2 Canons I and II, but it does not cite NDPA section 40, section 41, or the 72-hour deadline. Because the unsupported financial figures are central in D2 and D3, I applied the fabrication penalty and did not round upward.

name: Francisca Umejesi Nkeiruka
flagReason: Unsupported NDPR penalty, assumed revenue baseline, and combined financial exposure over 70 million Naira are used as impact facts.
feedback: D1 is very strong. It finds the expected technical issues: SQL injection, unsalted MD5, JWT alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing token expiry, stored XSS, missing Secure and SameSite cookie controls, open redirect, path traversal, and XXE. It also includes extra rows for username enumeration, role trust, sensitive data exfiltration, and excessive data exposure, but the core answer-key findings are present. The hash_equals decoy is correctly disproved in D1. D2 gives a complete chronological chain from recon to SQL injection, users.php access, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, and exfiltration. It includes CVSS vectors and a business-impact section, but it omits the failed password attempt, does not bring the JWT findings into the CVSS table, and uses a lower sample-based Naira estimate plus unsupported regulatory penalty assumptions. D3 has the right executive-report shape and useful SQLi plus XXE detection stopgaps, and its remediation order puts SQL injection first. The major D3 deduction is that it names the wrong decoy: it treats stored XSS not being initial access as the decoy instead of disproving Base64URL or hash_equals. It also omits several answer-key findings from the client-facing findings list and repeats the unsupported penalty and revenue assumptions. D4 is solid. It refuses the journalist, limits writing to evidence, escalates colleague-related timeline evidence, cites ISC2 Canons I and II, names the NDPC, and states a 72-hour notification duty. It still should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 explicitly and separate Commission notice from affected-subject notice. I applied the fabrication penalty for the unsupported penalty and revenue-based impact figures, so there was no humane upward rounding.

name: Adedayo Ogunsemoyin
flagReason: D2 and D3 use unsupported Naira impact figures and D3 treats the exploitable alg:none branch as the decoy instead of disproving the safe hash_equals or Base64URL construct.
feedback: D1 is excellent. It identifies SQL injection, unsalted MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing exp and nbf, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, and missing Secure and SameSite cookie controls, and it correctly explains that the hash_equals HMAC comparison is not the exploitable weakness. Only minor credit is lost for adding username disclosure and for some numbering confusion. D2 has a strong narrative chain with SQL injection, users.php access, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, and customer exfiltration. It also gives good metric justifications for SQL injection and stored XSS. The big scoring problem is the CVSS table: most rows use placeholders like CVSS:3.1/AV/AC/PR/UI/S/C/I/A rather than complete vectors, so the CVSS requirement is only partly met. D2 also overstates likely next targets such as .env, SSH keys, and cloud API keys, and the 69.3 million Naira impact is not traceable to the expected sample math. D3 is well written and client-friendly, with a clear executive summary, threat model, findings, remediation order, and detection stopgaps. However, it fails the D3 decoy requirement by calling the alg:none branch itself the construct examined and saying it is fully exploitable, instead of identifying the safe hash_equals or Base64URL construct. It also uses an unsupported 79.3 million Naira impact figure and makes BoltCash inheritance claims more strongly than the evidence permits. D4 is good: it refuses the journalist, documents only verified facts, handles colleague evidence through formal channels, cites ISC2 Canons I and II, and recognizes NDPC and affected-data-subject notification obligations. It should add the exact NDPA section 40 and section 41 references and the 72-hour deadline. I applied the fabrication penalty for unsupported impact figures and did not round up because the D3 decoy error is material.

name: Kazeem Habeeb
flagReason: D2, D3, and D4 use unsupported 195 million Naira exposure figures, and D3 introduces unsupported Django and shared-microservice risk framing.
feedback: D1 is a solid catalogue with good source anchoring. It correctly identifies SQL injection, unsalted MD5, JWT alg:none, missing exp and nbf, open redirect, missing Secure and SameSite cookie flags, the hardcoded sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 secret, and XXE. It also correctly rejects the hash_equals comparison as the decoy. The main deductions are that stored XSS and path traversal are missing as first-class findings, while role trust, username disclosure, and shared-auth scope take space that should have been used for the answer-key issues. D2 reconstructs a partial chain from SQL injection to users.php access, JWT alg:none, XXE, and customer exfiltration.
